A ROUND OF AMUSEMENT. —A circus. BE content with your lot, especially if it's a lot of money. "PAPA, what made Latin a dead language I" "It was talked to death, my son." • THE HORSE FOR EVERYBODY.—Ones own par- ticular "hobby." "MANKIND,' said a lecturer, "includes women, for man embracss woman." A SOCIABLE man is one who when he has ten minutes to spare goes and bothers somebody who hasn't. As ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure —that is to say, the druggist is likely to charge Just as much for it. "How do you like schoo!, Georgie, by this time ?" Georgie : "Oh, I don't mind the sollool It's the teacher that makes all the trouble." "The love of ilattery," says Swift, "in most men proceeds from the mean opinion they have of themselves; iii women from the contrary." IT is well known that some animals shed their coats in hot weather, but it has not been as generally remarked that excitable dugs leave oil their pants as the cold weather comes on. . " WE: ~" Said an Irish attse ney, " if it plaze the eoort, if I am wrong in this, I have another point that is equally conclusive." "CAN I have a poached egg ?” said a traveller, entering a transatlantic inn. " Yes, the negro waiter. "All our eggs are poached— leastways, our chickens are." STRANGIIR (to gravedigger) : " Who's (lead?" Gravedigger : " Ohl fgefeiz., 4irumbhes" " What complaint?" "No esisisiskint ; everybody it ssatisfi d." Weirs Freddy was seaseeti Ashy his engagement With Miss H. was broken off, he replied, " Oh, she turned out a deceiver." (Bat be did not mention that he was the deceiver she turned out). INNOCENT SAILCASM. Little Willie: "I wish I was you, Mr. Sellinade." Mr. Selfmade (who has -come to dinner) : " And why, Willie r Willie : "'Cause you don t get your ears pulled for eating with your knife." CAWS AND EFFECT.—" Disturbed by the noise of the rooks, old fellow? Take out your gun and have a shot at them. Remove the caws, and the effect will cease, you know." "HE is madly infatuated with her." "In- deed ?" "Yes. He even went so far as to tell her that if she were only a few years younger he would marry her." " WHY, Pat, you're never going to live in Sierra Leone! It's the white man's grave." "Well, show me the place where a man never dies, and I'll go and end my days there." HEART.—The best card in the chance game of matrimony; sometimes evercome by diamonds and knaves ; often won by tricks; and occasionally treated in a shuffling manner, and then cut alto- gether. At a recent theatrical performance, the pistol with which the heroine was to be murdered by the villain of the piece missed fire. Instead of losing his head, the deep-dyed scoundrel exclaimed furiously: "Die, then, the first victim of smokeless powder!" LAW PROFFSSOB. : "What constitutes burglary?" Student: "There must be a breakage." Law Professor: "Then if a.man enters a door and takes a sovereign from the waistcoat in the hah, would that be burglary?" Student: "Yes, sir; because that would break me."

LORD PALMERSTON was once at a prize fight 11 when a policemsn appeared on the scene. His 1 Lordship was then Prime Minister. The police- I man demanded his name, and got the reply, "Palmerston." Bobby gave a grin, and said, "Come along, old cove, you won't palm that off upon me." GEORGE THE FOURTH, on hearing someone say that Moore had murdered Sheridan in his life of that statesman, observed, " Well, I won't say that Mr. Moore has murdered Sheridan, but he has certainly attempted his life." A PRECOCIOUS INFANT.—Young Wife: "What is baby trying to say, dear ?" Husband: "Give it up. He seems to be trying to manufacture a word about twenty syllables long." Young Wife: " Isn't that lovely ! He'll be a great scientist some day !" "Will you allow me to look at your paper for a in -anent, sir," said a tramp, politely, to a gentle- man in the park. "I am anxious to ascertain the weather probabilities." "You are interested in the weather, then?" replied the gentleman, hand- ing over the paper. " Yes, sir. lam going to lie down and take a nap if the elements are in my favour." THE RIGHT PLACE.—" And, mamma," sobbed the unhappy wife, " he—he threw hie slippers ...cross the r-room, and t-told me to go to the 800-boo "He did, the brute! Then you did right, my dear child, to come straight home to me." Jolts: " sayin', Jean, when ye gang tea the market the morn, dim'a buy ony mair barrels o' apples frae Taanson." Jean : " Whit's th' mAitter wi"ra.mson, John? Dis he nae pit the big apples at the Lop an' the wee anes at the bottom? John: "Ota.ay ; but he disna mark the tap, an' I've opened three o' his barrels at the bottom tae show the customers." ' AFTER all, there is not much difference between ' a very hungry man and a very gluttonous one. The one longs to eat; the other eats too long. That's all. CRITIC: "I tell you what it is, Mr. M‘Daub ; those ostriches are simply superb. You shouldn't paint anything but birds." Artist (disgusted): "Those are not ostriches. They are angels !" A MEDITATIVE American has made a great dis- covery. He says that there are two principal reasons why people do not mind their own - business. One is that they have not got any business, and the other is that they have not got any mind. A VERY illiterate man, who could neither read nor write, took up a paper and held it upside down, with the result that in an illustration a coach appeared to be topsy-turvy. "Bill," said the man to a friend, "herd's a frightful haceident to a coach! Bead about it, will yer?" Countryman : "My goodne33 ! Why, then, a fellow hasn t time to logk round the town !" div.p: CAP ITA "

Whatever.truth there may be in the alleged intentions of some Americans to lodnap the intant son of Le Duke and Duchess of York, there is no doubt that the Royal baby has ben constantly "shadowed " by a detective from So-tland-yard. If there is any foundation for the idea, the plot must by this time be exploded by the publicity which has been given to it. According to one of the Sunday papers, the Americans came to this country with the object of kidnapping the child of a certain American millionaire who has made this country his home, and who is is not; a persona g-sata with hosts of people of all classes in the United States. The object of the conspirators was, of course, the handsome reward with which the restoration of the baby would be purchased. Foiled in that object, they are alleged to have turned their thoughts to- wards the latest addition to the Royal line. The gang are said to carry on kidnapping in the States as their special chosen branch of villainy, and if experience has made them adepts at their work their game so far has been frustrated here.

M. Ferdinand de Lesseps, whose death at the:age of 89 is announced, will be remembered as the author of the greatest. engineering success and the greatest enuineering failme of the nineteenth cen- tury. The idea of cutting a channel between the Meuiterranean and the Red Sea was entertained long before XI. de Lessens took it up: it was entirely due to his energy and skill that the task was carried out. lie had much to fight aguinst,not 'he least being the determined hostility of ' the French Government. "Le Grand Francais " was just as confident about the Paxama as he was about the Suez Canal; but the attempt to dig a channel between the Atlantic and the Pacific Oceans led to one of the greatest political and commercial scandals of the age.

The Brigg election has revived speculation as to prospects at the next general election. So far as the Liberals are concerned tbe view Wren by good, responsible men is that we hai I gain seats in Eng- land, but lose them in Scotland, while in Wales we are sure. Conservatives are both amused and angry at the " explanation " which Mr. Stanley Boulter gives of the result of the election. Mr. BoUlter's assertion that Mr. Chamberlain's scheme—of which Mr. Boulter claims to he the criginator—for enabl- ing the working classes to become the owners of their houses, won the seat for Mr. llic.Tharla.m, is simply laughed to scorn at the Carlton Club.

I am glad to see a tendency to lay emphasis on the enormous electoral advantage that would accrue to the Liberal party by playing " one man one vote " as its trump card in the last trick of the rubber before the general election. The matter has been taken up in various quarters, and on Monday we were reminded that " it was the view of the shrewdest Liberal wire-puller of on: generation that nothing would ever really rouse the country against., the Lords except a franchise question, and it was his opinion, therefore, that the cup would never be full until it included 'one man one vote.'" I am glad to be on the side of the shrewdest Liberal wire-puller, though, indeed, it needs no extraordinary shrewdness to see that what concern* every voter in the kingdom without exception appeals to an enormously larger area than questions which, however important, affect sections of the nation only,like Irish land, Welsh Disestablishment, or London unification. A revival of the obl cry for shorter Parliaments and the repeal of the Septennial Act, has received powerful advocacy as the ace to be kept up the Liberal sleeve. I doubt the existence of sufficient enthusiasm for more frequent elections to make this a vital and telling cry, but so long as every constituency is liable to the irritation felt to-day by lr. Peeltitt's 4,300 supporters in Brigg at finding themselves outvoted by non-residents, so long will one man one vote be a live and poteat demand.

We hear sn much from time to time of the quarrels he.ween author,".and publiolers that. it is distinctly r4rt.shing to com- across illustrations which point in a directly opro.ite way. Gibbon, refe-ring to his solitude in the heart. of London when engov.ed on - the "Decline and Fall," Pays he was often proud end happy when he could prevail on his bookseller, Peter Elra,.lev. to en'iren dulness of the even- int. Gibbon's letters further testifN to the re7ard in which he h,ld not only F.lnasley but &so Cadell, the publisher. One of these letters. a superb speci- men of a most rare antcgraph and 1 believe hitherto unpubliShed, hrs just bPen under the hammer at Sotheby's and sold for £lB 10.. It is a very long letter, the four paces quarto being vPry closely written. The date is Nin.rcli 28, 1789, when Gibbon was at Lausanre. Like many other authors, the historian felt a more than .rdinary curiosity in wl'at was beitri said about his books. Tie antici- pate. abuse, for "the best. men'. and the most sue- , cessful writer must hear many things, perhaps j many truths, offensive to his vanity."

Lord Russell is doing his best. to improve the lot of the British jurvman. Hitherto, when cnseq have been settled without the jury being swotn,the twelve men in the hos:. have had no fees. But the Lord Cl.ief Justice has inaugurated a rule that whereT they have been called,' and where their services are material to the settlement, at issue,the jury shall be paid whether sworn or not. On Tues- day morning a jury was empanelled to try ft breach of promise case against n Mr. Crossland, but the matter was settled after counsel had conferred, the defndant undertaking to Pay the lady—said to he an actress—£3so and costs. To the latter Lord Russell insisted on }wino' added twelve guineas for the jury; and Sir Edward Clarke, for the defend- ant, assented. This is a practice which may be fol- lowed by other judges.

Mr. Blake, who arrived from Canada a few years nco to assist the Trish Nationalists in fighting their cause in Parliament. has !onn become either home- sick or disgusted with the Ffon.e of Commons. TTis first appearance at the Eic.hty Club will still he re- membered. Fe had not than been heard in Parlia- ment. and. from the official position he held in Canada. crent were the exnectations both of Trish Nationalists and English Liberals regarding him. The appearance he then made was disoppnintinsz, but be has proved himself to he a man of enormous voluhility and of an impartial cast of mind. The main effort in Parliament was to give to the Tlome Rule agitation a eimptittltionnl character, and to: support it by constinnal reasons derived from Canadian example and experience. Beyond this he proved rather a failure in the rfortse. UP was not intimately familiar with the details of Trish griev- , tutees. and when his con,titutional arguments were no longer applicable to the questions Under con- sideration he was 'doomed to silence, and a good , i Nationalist tradesman proved a more serviceable champion of the Trish (muse than Mr. Blake. Ile has, no doubt. found out his inherent wentrn..s.and he will hear with satisfaction the announcement of a general election, which will allow him to return to the country where he has earned his laurels.

A news agency has issued a telegram stating thrit. it is efficially informed that Parliament. will meet on the sth of February. This is a little earlier than ' has been lately surmised. hut it. is still so late that the week or ten days' anin which the Government will reap by it will not. affect the legislative for- tunes of the session as I have sketched them. Unionist papers make some fun of the parliamen- tary work beinr, dependent, in the midst o a greet crisis. on the kitchen end the hairdres.ing end bath accommodation. About the necessity of the kitchen no question can he raised, if the country is to bn protected during the dinner hour from a snatched victory by either side in n thin Tlonse. The other two are luxurious additions which cannot. he so well defended. hut some epicurean being must lin., fel"- the want of them. end he must have had suffi- cient influence with the Government to induce nu!- flinty-hearted Chancellor of the Exchequer to open hi A purse-strings even to the e-ri ent of the few thousand pounds which their construction would require.

The Countess of Warwick has decided to stand at the approaching election's as a candidate for a seat on the Warwick Board of Guardians. Mrs- Ta.bitha Whitman, Mumfordville, Ky., Is ninety.two years old, and ll' r latest experience is t) have a needle taken out o ner elbow. It was one which she had swallowed ti .rty years ago.—American parer. The wife of the present J +panese Minister in Berlin, the Viscountess Aoki, is of Orertnan birth, and is a per- sonal frierd of the Empn•or William. This marriage of a German lady to a Japanese gentleman has proved a most happy one. They have one child—little Hana— who is remarkably beautiful. If, when grown to woman- hood, she re'ains all the grace aud loveliness she now possesses, she will be one of the most beautiful women in the world. 4! Woman" hears that Prince Henry of Battenberg is determined that his daugh' er shall be brought up to he really useful. and that when she is old enough she is to be instructed in the work of the Royal kitchen. One of the smallest of eaters must be Mr. Herbert Spencer. The modern Aristotle has crept into the seven- ties tv giving his digestive organs as little to do as possible. He told a writer in " Answers," who inter- viewed him wine years ago on the subject of the L.C.C., "That what is known as a good dinner would kill me outright." Prince Georqe of Greece visited America some few years ago, ,nd a lady who made the return pas,age in the same steamer says that he had an unpleasant time, owing to the attentions of a large number of American ladies. Nearly all had cameras, and lurked about seek- ing to take "snap-shots" at his face. Nearly a hund- red such appliances were levelled at him whenever he came on deck. At last he adopted the expedient of holding his hands before his face ; but finding this a little too fatiguing, he actually remained below during the latter part of the voyage.

A Welsh Gift to the Empress of Russia. One of the most unique gifts that the now Emprawi of Russia received on . her marriage was a beautiful paper knife from the coal miners of Roabon,in Wales. made of jet-black enal. Two years ago the Princess, when visit- ing near Rtia.bnn, descended one of the coal pits,and as no notice of her intention had been given, special gar- ments could nnt he provided. It is said that a rough flannel shirt, a pair or new csriurov trousers, a blue necktie, and a cloth cap made up the coqume of the lady who is now Empress of all the Russias. On her return from the mine the Princess looked lovely, her eyela.shez. heavily darkened with coal-dust which con- tratf d with her delicate rose-leaf complexion.

An Insidious Invasion. There are signs and tokens of the insidious approach of crinoline, more narticularly in the new evening. dresses. The sk;rts of these are immensely wide, and a quantity of satin. velvet, or brocade has to be used in producing the requiAite " ripnling " effect. As a natural cnrsequence, cheap dressmakers, whose nlients are obliged to study economy, use all sorts of stiffened lin- ings, stuff out the folds at the back with horsehair, and insert a ,vire within the hem. Whither do all these devices tend ? Towards crinoline, most unmistakably. But at present it is merely drifting. Smart women are as vet unconscious of the direction in which Paris men- milliners are forcing matters. If they begin to realise it, perhaps the danger may yet be averted.

A Lady Sea. Captain. Lady (Spencer) Clifford, widow of Sir Robert Caven- dish Spencer Cliffcrd, lon. Yeoman Usher pf the Black Rod, has opened the way to a. new profession for women by being chartered as " captain " under the Board of Trade, by which she has absolute command of a vessel of her Awn. Always fo,d of a life under "white wings." and finclin' in yachting the only solace to a severe domestic affliction, L,dy Clifford made several cruises to Norway and Scily in her yacht, commanded by a competent captain; but, a 4 many women have found in other circumstances, she found the divided authority of the owner and the captain hardly wo-ked well. Lady Clifford obtained the position of captain, the first woman in England who has ever obtained it, ard• with a good sailimr master under her, navigNted a 350-ton yocht in the Channel and Mediterranean with such succi-ss that. she proposes sh ortly to visit the East in the same manner.
WHICH LEG BROKE DOWN?
Any stool will stand on three legs, but not on two. Tbere must st least be three points to balance. _ _
The three legs a human life stands on are these—blood, brains, and breath. Or, as the doctors put it, the cir- culation, the nerves, and the respiration. Let one of these three legs fail and ye fall.

Yet, unlike the legs of a stool, the three supports of a human life are connected together. When one weak.ns it weakens the others. If a man's blood is had his brains and breath will suffer. And so if the fault with the brains or the breath. They are a kind of Trinity—three phases of one life—one life running through three channels. And how strangely they blend or part.

Listen to this "if ant ole knocked at the door," says a woman," it would startle me and set lny heart flutter- ing and thumping until I could not breathe." Here were the nerves, the blond, and the breath comhinine• t,maee mischief. What lee. of the tl:ree weakened first? To find this out we shall have to ask her to tell more of her experience and then draw a conrin:iol. _ _

We quote from a letter of hers dated August 8-h,1892. We read her words with interest, for we cannot say when her trouble may be our trouble. "It was at Michaelmas of 1880." she says, "that I first felt weak and weary. My mouth tasted bad'''. and I was oppressed with a gnawing, sinking feeling at the pit of the stomach. I could eat but littls, and what I did eat gave me a sense of pain and fullness at the chest and sides. Also I had a great pain at the heart Rad palpitation, and brought up a nasty sour fluid into my moufb.
"InJannary of the next year I removevi to a houßp

• in Thurlow-road, which was damp; I took cold, and my trouble grew worse. At first I had a dreadtul cough which gave me no rest night or day, and almost shook me to pieces. The fits of coughing would last for two hours at a time, and I would retch and threw up frothy phlegm until I was 'sick and exhausted. After a time my breathing became so difficult I had to he pronped up in bed, and for hours I would lie gasping for breath. I had night sweats an had that my linen and pillows were wet in the morning. 0-sing to the cough and the short- nes; of brpath,l got little or no sleep at night for weeks together and could barelv -tand or walk about. " I struggled on as heat I could, my neighbours kindly assisting me. I got so nervous that if anynne merely knocked at the door it would set my heart fluttering and thumping until T could not breathe. People said I consumption, and would never get well. II ad lost all faith in doctors and physic, and did not care how soon the end Cattle. is Whit in this condition sod fan. drifting t grave (in May, 1881), my I usband heard of Mother Seigel'e Curative Syrup and persuaded me to try it. Without a particle of confidence that it would help me I I began taking it nevertheesS, and in a few weeks my appetite returned and my food digested and strenwhened me. The tide had turned. Soon the cough, the niekt sweats, and the' palpitation left me. Presently I was VITELL ;-011 none but those whojhave sufferedjas I did know what that ward means. I thank God I took Mother SPiZers Srran. It surely saved my You *lay publish what I say if you choose, and I will Iris dip answer inquiries. I am a dressmaker, and have lived in this neighbourhood twenty-eight years. (Signed) Mrs. H. Radford, Great Bradley, nearliewmarket, Aug. 18th, 1892." What is the inference from these facts!? Which leg of the stool first gave way in this case? The blond. But not of itse'f. The poison of a disorganised and dis- tempered stomach entered the circulation. disturbed the heart and lungs, and set up the other alarming symp- toms. There 'was no organic heart disease, no ern- gumption. Yet how many (doctors, too) are thus deceived. The remedy she finally used did away with the cause—indigestion and dyspepia—and recovery fol- lowed. Is there not in this wonderful cure a lecoion and rational hope for all who are similarly afflicted?

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

MY DEAREST NELLIE, • Day by day we are made more aware of the fact that the winter season is close upon us. The • rapidly shortening days, that suggesli gloom and dreariness, have their complement, however, in the comfort derived from cosy firesides; whil,3 to us women in particahr the ont-of•door world assumes a pleasing asp9o.; front the brightnesi that is presented everywhere by the sho:i-winclows. Decked with fill the fastiinating trifles which gladden th.) hea•ec of the average woman, they demonstrate the fe.htthv. th,3 'or, he the season advances, the more novel arc the fie,j,n3. I saw a capital c,./at, the o%hec dAy. it is made of golden tan-faced c!oth, with velvet sleeves. The collars and fronts are of sable, fitting back toad straight wrapped over tlle fronts. A large seal- skin hat with sable tails goes very well with this costume.

Despite the fact that we arc getting on into the winter, a quantity of light lace is used to trim hate and bonnets, and gives a delicate, if unseasonable, appearance to fells and velvets. The Tam o' Seanter is a favourite shape in velvet jatted with sequins and trimmed with feather plumes, or fashioned in cloth to match the drev and having a border of fur, with two quills stul through a buckle, in real Scotch style. Modern millinery admits of many incongruous combieatiors of ma- terials and colours. One of the Y.attst Inee to which the pretty, delicate chiffon is put, is to trim felt and velvet hats. Roeettee and puff., of chiffon are mixed with squirrel tails, velvet roses, and lace on large erections of felt, beaver, or velvet. This winter's hats are certainly preferred small. They are in toque and eapote and are much trimmed with jet, velvet, anri flowers. In fact, many are formed or. fl eee• a, with just a little coronet form or outline je or velvet. White and lightecoloured felt hats al-, worn with blacit trimming, and Ri...•iculazly dainty is the contrast of black and white. amnete are trimmed more than they h.s.ve been with bows and feathers, and the trimming is brought forward. A pretty hat-boneet for a child of from two to six is made of white Frenol, felt, trimmed with ostrich tips and white satin ribbons.

How convenient are many ex;eing falhions, and how infinitely one may vary teem wthu ex3eed- ing the limits of good style ! An irrimence amount of different materials awl colours are used in gowns, though it ie true in many instances of colour combinations artistic merit i 2 not a promni- mut feature. A plain, well cut skirt under a cloth cape enables the wearer to come and go without attracting undesirable attention, yet the moment she enters a house the clos.it can Ls oast en one side and a smart little bodice revealei, imparting just that amount of festive appearance that is desirable.

Chinchilla is being very mach worn round the bottoms of fancy silk gowns, and a fur to whio'i the name of smoked fox has been given is also popular. Real silver fox is in great favour, an very charming it is, but costly. Glinchilla capes or collets and muffs are very pretty and look extremely good, but the fur muss be real if any wear is to be had out of it. No skin is more et:sUy or cheaply imitated, but the ina:alion soon looh. patchy and ragged. Light Russian sable is he- quently seen, and mink, petnis, or mock sable, >l4 it is called, abroad and at home, is very charm- lag made up into muffs and triannhags. There is a peculiarly good and rich look about all the furs shown in London thiA year, as if the animals from which they were taken were in pecniiarly gooi condition when trapped. For una its boas and muffs fox is very fashionable. One of the latest boas is made of dark smoked fox, with spring head, and a medium-sized muff to match may be worn with great effect.

Almost) all ttimmings take the term cf elongated Vandykee, that can be placed in any desired position. A vast majariv of them are made in jet, as it can be applied ut co many ways, and a great many people will wear smart black all through the coming winter. For ovening attire they are worked on gold net over coloured sada in gold threai, with tiny fiat round discs of gold, aluminium, mother- of-pearl, or coloured xylorite, mingled with pearl, crystal, and iridescent heads. In some places the satin is out away, and there are bundry modes of giving effect.
Yours lovingly, JENN IL.

THE DOUBLE LIFE: 08., THE HAMPTON MYSTERY. By the Author of "DARKWOODs"
CHAPTER XLV. IN THE TOILS. I see thou art implacable, more deaf To prayers than winds and seas; yet winds and
seas Are reconciled at length, and sea to shore: Thy anger, unappeasable, still rages, Eternal tempest never to be calm.

MILTON. Unconscious of the deadly enemies creeping up stealthily behind them in the mist and the dark- ness on that lonely, deserted street, Giralda and little Fay hurried onward toward the doctor's residence, conversing in low tones as they went. As they gained the nearest street corner—that by which Adlowa's hired horses were in waiting— & gust of wind seized their umbrella, threatening to turn it inside out.

"Wait a moment, Fay," said Giralda, pausing to right the umbrella and to gather her waterproof cloak closer. "The night is worse than I thought. I do not like to expose you to the wind and rain. We will go back, darling." "Oh, no, no," urged Fay, pleadingly. "Yon want to know how the sick man is. The doctor has been to see him again to-day. Let us go 0n.,, Giralda allowed herself to be persuaded, her OM anxieties urging her strongly in the same direction.
The refractory umbrella was reduced to a con. dition of usefulness, and the young pair were . . .

about to resume their walk, when A'alOwe gave a signal, and in an instant the two men had sprung upon their prey. There was a woman's gasping cry, a child's low, frightened moan, and Giralda and Fay, helpless and terrified, were clutched close in the hands of their captors. "Not a word—not a cry, Giralda I" whispered Lord Adlowe, fiercely. "You know who I am. At the first sound you make to summon assistance, I will choke your brother as remorselessly as I would crush a worm !" Giralda repressed the scream that trembled on her lips. Her brain was in a whirl. She could not think. She knew only that her enemy had found her out, and that she was again in his power. More thoughtful of another than of herself even now, she stretched out her arms to encircle her brother, as if determined to defend him with her life.

"Put the boy into the wagon, Wigby," com- manded Adlowe, keeping a close hold upon Gir- alda, and a keen watch up and down the street. Little Fay, more dead than alive, was deposited In the wagon. "Bind him !,' said Adlowe, briefly. Wigby hastened to tie the little fellow's ankles together, and then secured his wrists in like man- ner. "Oh, do not take him without me !" cried Gir- alda, Fay's low, quivering moans rending her heart.

" I don't intend to," declared Adlowe, his voice thrilling with his savage exultation. "You shall go with him. You shall be in a measure his guar- dian, for upon your conduct shall depend his life. I am a desperate man, Giralda, and I am in a mood for desperate deeds. Let me help you into the wagon." Giralda hesitated, flashing a wild glance through the darkness and the thin, slow-falling rain. No one was in the street at that moment. The shops were closed, and their proprietors had retired to their back parlours. There was no one to hear her if she should call.

Half-stunned and half-fainting, she submitted to be helped into the wagon. "Shall I bind the young lady," my lord ?" asked Wigby. "No, it is not necessary," replied Adlowe. "You have only to place the boy within my reach. If she chooses to escape, she will only seal his doom." Giralda sank down on the cushioned seat, and Wigby covered her and Fay with lap-robes, then descended to the pavement. "Go at once to the bluff cottage and bring Mrs. Bittly, Wigby," said his lordship, in an undertone. "You had better be on your way to the station. I can manage my passengers alone." He .mounted to his seat, took the reins, and drove slowly down the street, Wigby hurrying on foot in the direction of the station. For a time Giralda did not speak, seeming wholly benumbed. She sought out poor little Fay's bound wrists, and clasped his hands in her own, but his low, frightened sobs and moans were almost more than she could bear. She laid her face against his little tear-wet cheek, and drew him close to her, .but she could not soothe him with words. Adsowe hurried out of the town by the shortest route, having informed himself in advance in re- gard to his course. His evil soul thrilled with ex- ultation at his success in his night's work, and he began to indulge a hope that he should yet re- trieve his sinking fortunes and attain to the wealth he so much coveted. The rough town pavements were soon left be- hind, and the wheels rolled almost noiselessly over the country road upon which they had en- tered. The mist continued to fall slowly, and through it, as through a haze, Giralda saw houses and trees loom up on either side, and now and then a light flashed cut from some parlour window, and the sound of music and laughter strayed to her ears, sseming to mock her with a happiness which she feared she was never to know again. After a while, rousing herself from her despair, she broke the silence. "Lord Adlowe," she said in a low voice, "where are you taking us?" Adlowe started as from a reverie, and answered promptly: "To a house which I have hired under an as- sumed name near Pesicoed." "For what purpose ;" "You know as well as I do, Giralda—to compel you to become my wife. This house at Pencoed is merely intended as a temporary retreat. I mean to keep you there until the search for you is over, and your spirit is broken sufficiently to make you suhmit to my will. In the hour in which you promise to marry me I will give you your free- dom. Till then you will be my prisoner. He spoke with a determination that made Gir- alda shudder. "You have nicely outwitted me so far," he con- tinued, with R. hitter emphasis. "hut von qnd mow was a young girt iure_you is no match for a desperate man like me. You have not compre- hended what you were fighting." "You spoke of a search for me," said the young girl. "Who is searching for me ?" "Lord Trevelyan. You may imagine why he Is searching for you, since he hates and loathes you now, believing in your baseness and treach- ery," answered Lord Adlowe, delighting in the falsehood he was uttering. "I believe his lord- ship has some idea of prosecuting you for trying to obtain money of him under false pretences." "I never obtained money of him under false pretences," exclaimed Giralda indignantly. "You didn't go to his house under an assumed name and an assumed identity, and allow him to make a will leaving you a fortune, eh ;" asked Adlowe, mercilessly. "That is the way he states the case." A low, crivering sigh came from Giralda. The hot salt tears sprang to her burning eyes. "I loved him I" she murmured under her breath, bending low over her little brother. "I truly and sincerely loved him." -4‘ Then," said Adlowe, coolly, "Lord Grosvenor has turned against you. He can't stand all the disgrace and scandal that would ensue from his alliance with a daughter of Geoffrey Trevelyan. The marquis infected him with his own sentiments, and he has gone to town, determined to spend a gay season and to contract a more suitable mar- riage—" "You speak falsely, Lord Adlowe !" interrupted Giralda, in a sudden glow of indignation greater than that she had displayed before. "I know Lord Grosvenor Vic) well to believe what you may say of him." "Oh, very well. I hardly expected yen to be- lieve it. Cherish your little delusions, Giralda, while you can." He spoke carelessly, as if her faith or want of faith in Lord Grosvenor mattered little to him. His manner went far to convince Giralda a his truthfulness. Her exp rinse() of the world of late had not been such as to continue her childlike trust in human nature, and for a moment she acknowledged to herself, with a dull pang at her heart, that it was very possible that Lord Gros- venor might have been persuaded to relinquish all preteusions to the hand of Geoffrey Trevelyan's daughter. But only for a moment did she consider such a possibility. Then her faith and trust in Paul Grosvenor overrode all possibilities and objec- tions, and stood as firm and unassailable as a

"Say nothing more to me of Lord Grosvenor," she said, sternly, her blue eyes flashing. "I do not believe a word you say. lam not even sure but that Lord Trevelyan would forgive me for my crime of being the daughter of his nephew, and would cease my father's persecutions for my make." _

Adlowe winced, but made no reply. There followed a silence, during which his lord- ship drove more swiftly. ventinz his secret annoy- ance upon the liorbes. Giralda bent lower over Fay. His head was in her lap, closely sheltered with her cloak and the lap-robe. He was awake, and softly crying, his young soul convulsed with a vague terror of what was to befall his sister and himself. 41 yr Int

"My darling I my darling ?" whispered Giralda, Lthering him closer to her bosom, and softly kiss- ig him, "do not grieve so! God will take cars of .s, dear Fay. Cap't you trust in Him ?" The boy clung to her without replying Giralda stole her hand under the robe and gently began to pull at the bonds that confined his wrists.

A wild hope sprang up in her soul. If she could free Fay, and escape with him from the rear end of the wagon, and crouch somewhere in the dark- ness and so elude her enemy 1 The idea was less wild than it might seem. The wagon was of a style very common, having a driver's seat, on which Adlowe sat, and in the rear of this two other seats running lengthwise, and shut in by a little door. It was upon one of these rear seats the captives sat, Fay being within reach of Adlowe's hand. Fay swiftly comprehended Giralda's intent, and hushed his sobs.

Adlowe looked quietly over his shoulder. Giralda worked silently, picking at the knot; but Wigby had done his work well. The heavy rope resisted all her efforts. Fay motioned her to put her ear to his lips. She did so, and he whispered: "I've a knife in my pocket. Cut the cord!" Giralda's hand stole toward his pocket in quest of the knife.

And at that moment AdLowe reached over, start- ling them both beyond measure. "I see what you are about!" he said coolly. "Trying tD escape? No, no, Giralda, you won't outwit me again ! " He stopp,d the horses, and regardless of the pleadings of his captives, lifted the lad and put him on the front seat beside himself, wrapping him carefully from the rain. "And now, Gira.lda," he continued, starting the horses again, "you may escape when you please. Bnt if you do escape you will be sealing your brother's fate !"

His tone made the girl shudder, "Lord Adlowe," she cried,- with passionate earnestness," is there no pity in your heart? Fay and I have never hatmed you. I beg you to let us go—" "Never harmed me !" repeated Adlowe, mock- ingly. "Why, it is you two and your brother who have come between me and the finest property in England." "We will pay you a ransom to let us go," pleaded Giralda. "I will promise you any sum you may ask for our freedom. My mother will pay it—" " The ransom I ask is yourself r rejoined Adlowe, interrupting her. "I loved your mother, the Lady Beatrice, and spent the best years of my life in useless devotion to her. That love has turned to hatred. It would wring her heart to have her only daughter become my wife, and to be compelled to dower her out of the fortune I expected to receive with her ladyship. Geotirey bates me, and it would be a tine reveuge on him to make his daughter my wife. In short, Giralda, everything inspires me to this course, and not the least inspira- tion is yourself. Your beauty, your freshness, your innocence have charmed a heart- that was world- weary. lam not sure but that I even prefer you to the queenly, haughty Lady Beatrice ' "Do you not insult me *WI your professions of love,' said Giralda, creeping nearer, that she might comfort Fay. "I would rather have your hatred than your love!" " Tffere may be not so much difference between the two !" said Adlowe. "My love and my hatred are equally fierce, and not to be balked. Have you thought, Giralda, or are you too ignorant of the worlds usuages to consider the question, that this night's excursion with me will compromise your reputation, and cause Lord Grosvenor, despite his faith in you, to decline a marriage with you? I merely wish to show youthat, even were you aree, he would never marry you." Giralda was silent.

"I inn not so bad a man as you think me," con- tinue his lordship, after a pause. "I have been driven to desperation by finding myself likely to become a beggar, after years of expectancy and waiting to boeome my uncle's heir. But I have qualities which only need cultivating to make me h noble man. Giralda,, I love•you ! I worship you as a superior being I I should be as clay in your hands. You could mould me to your will. It is no light thing to pos.ess the power you do. You can make me good and honourable. You can drive me to v.•ieliednes mid baseness. I throw the re- sponsibility upon you--" " And I reject it ! " cried Giralda. " You cannot put upon another the responsibility Heaven placed upon you. If you have any desire to be- come good, show it by setting us free !" " I cannot do that. I love you too much. Have pity, Giralda, upon my erring soul that needs a guide, and become my guide to truth and good- ness." His hypocritical pretences disgusted the young girl. "It's a pity money is so hard to be got, Lord Ad!owe"' she said. "It must fatigue you to pre- tend to a repentance you do nut feel, if you were in earnest in your pretended desire to reform' a clergyman would be your best guide and counsellor. If you have any sense remaining," she added, "you muut see that it would be impossible for me to marry the enemy ot ny parents, the man but for whom my life and that of those dear to me would have been bright and cloudless. It is you, Lord AdlOwe, who stabbed my uncle Trevelyan so many years ago, and managed so that the crime and the odium were laid to my poor father I Marry you I should feel as if I were marrying my father's murderer, for you were the assassin vf his reputa- tion, which he held dearer .than life I Marry you Never ' Her indignant scorn held Adlowe silent. He could not answer her, and became sullen, thought- ful and plotting. The night wore on. Little Fay dropped asleep, his head falling upon the knee of his enemy. Giralda sat wakeful among the robes, her pale face upturned to the mist, her eyes striving in vain to pierce the dull gray of the clouded sky. What were her thoughts and prayers in that time of darkness her stern silence did not betray. Toward morning the mist cleared, but the chilly air grew keener and colder. Giralda shivered, in Spite of her wrappings. " We are almost there," said A4lowe, about day- break, breaking the long silence. " You will soon be at your new home, which you will leave, as I said, only when you promise to become my wife." ( 7'o be continued).

ATTACK ON A LONDON LADY.
HOW IT OCCURRED-HER DESCRIPTION OF THE CIRCUM- STANCES, AND THE OVERWHELMING TESTIMONY OF PROMINENT WITNESSES.

Mrs. W. Priest's statement of this ferocious attack is so extraordinary that some readers might think it in- credible, or that she was deceived by appearances, but her lamentable condition was admitted by her local doctor and corroborated by the physician in charge at the West London Hospital, and her sufferings were witnessed not only by Mrs. Fryett and Mrs. Waller, of Magdala Cottages, but by all of her immediate friends and neighbours. Consequently it is not to he wondered that our interviewer left her thoroughly convinced of the truth of her statements, which should be placed before the public. In fact what shd suffered and endured, 11( r narrow escape from death is the talk of tha suburb, and her home (4, Magdala Cottages, Wellington-road. Hounslow), has been besieged by friends offering con- gratulations, Her own statement, made September 8, 1894.—" During the early part of last year I was suffer- ing with Bright's Disease of the Kidneys, originating from a simple cold, and after being attended by my family doctor in Hounslow for some considerable time, he infermed me that he could not do me any good. I ' then became an in-patient of the West London Hospital for 11 weeks ; one of the physicians of that institution telling me that he could not possibly do me any good. I. was then discharged as incurable, and my family and friends gave up all hopes of my ever again being well. By this time dropsical swelling was such that no one who saw me thought my recovery possible, extending from :my ankles to my entire body. To make matters worse, after my return from the hospital I caught a fresh cold, which brought on bronchitis and pleurisy. I again called a local doctor, but derived no benefit from a month's further treatment. I suffered excrucia- ting pain in the shoulder-blades, pains shooting through me, even when sitting and lying, and my strength seemed exhausted. At this period, my father (Mr.A. Brown, mace-bearer of the Corporation ,Chequer, Devizes), who can vouch for my statement, sent me a bottle of Warner's "Safe" Cure, and after taking the second dose I felt relief ; by the time I had finished the contents of the bottle I felt quite another woman. I continued taking it, the relief being so marked that I eagerly looked for the time to come round for each sue- ceding dose. And after taking 15 bottles lam glad to say I am perfectly cured. It is with gratitude and heartfelt thanks I tender my testimony of the efficiency of Warner's "Safe" Cure. and I shall never fail to recommend it to all my friends and others whm I can."-

MACMILLAN AND CO.—A charming reproduction of the world-famed " Gulliver's Travels " has its origin in the now popular Cranford series. Illus- trations by C. E. Brock are scattered profusely through the book which needs no other embeliiBll- ment. Nothing could be truer or more imaginative than these admirable portrayals of characters and scenes in the travels. To describe the travels and their vivid reality would te superfluous since Gulliver has become so femous. but a satisfactory and interesting description of the author is given at the commencemenaand for the masterly manner of dealing with which, we are indebted to Henry .Graik. The publisher also has a few particulars of Culliver'e birth-place, etc. to add. Of the general get-up of the book everyone who has seen a speci- men of the Cranford series will be well acquainted without any special description.—Another of the series commenced by Mr. Crawford's "Love in Idleness" is represented by "The Rubies of St. Lo" by Charlotte M. Yonge. The story is light and • conversational and being short is very suitable for passing away a quiet hour. It deals with the traditional hiding of the rubies at the time of Henry VI. for the purpose of keeping them out of the hands of enemies. All trace of them becomes lost until near the conclusion of this interesting novel, when an accident and an explanatory note by an ancestor of the St. Lo'B. reveals their hiding place.—The price is as usual, 28. W. H. ALLEN AND CO.—What is known as "The Waterloo edition" of "Little Women and Little Women Married." Louisa M. Alcott's popular book, has just been published. This superb edition is an exact reproduction of that formerly issued at 18s., with its gilt-edged paper and unrivalled letter- press. Of its undoubted excellence and cheapness too much cannot be said. A book of 600 pages with these excellent qualifications, and illustrations by Frank T. Merrill, is inordinately cheap at 6s. T. FISHER UN WIN AND CO.—The "Century Maga- zine" for December has its prominent feature in another "animal" tale by Budyard Kl3ling.entitled "The Walking Delegate." Instead of taking India for his "camping ground" the author in this amus- ing tale has chosen the wide field of America. A splendid reproduction of "The Madonna of the Donors" by Van Dyck is engraved by T. Cole from tbe painting in the Louvre, and serves as frontis- piece. Other original and interesting stories suit- able for Christmas reading are included in this number. CAESELL AND CO.—lt Will be with undis- guised pleasure that the general public receive .the intimation that Cassell's Family Magazine, which has held the leading place amongst the illustrated Magazines for the past twenty years, has come down in price and gone up in excellence. It is printed on new and clearer type, and various oth or improve- ments mark the commencement of the new series. The literary and artistic attractions for next year will be of an even higher quality that at anyprevi- ous period. A new design illustrates the cover and the price now is 64.—" Picturesque America" has now reached its 21st part and the December num- ber deals with the grandeur and beauty of the Yosemite valley and is splendidly illustrated. A charming frontispiece represents an old time picture of the city of Cleveland.—Part 50 of Cassell's Natural History edited by Dr. P. M. Duncan, F.R.S, has for its subject, various types of fish, to better illustrate the appearance of which, several pictures are given.—" Our Earth and its story "does not de- teriorate as the numbers increase, for part 23 is as much a type of excellence as was the first number; the "story's" special feature being the splendid tinted engraving which prefaces each number. GEORGE NEWNES AND CO.—This month brings with it the double number of the Strand Magazine containing 208 pages and 320 illustrations. The number is certainly one calculated to interest, amuse, and instruct people of both sexes and all ages and sizes, for everything in it is first-class. Among the items included in the magazine are an interesting interview with Mr. [Dram Maxim, by J. Bucknall Smith, coupled with illustrations from photographs; caricaturists and their work by Ray- mond Blathwayt,and illustrations by some of theme athletes of the year with photographic illustrations; stories by Dr. A.Conan Doyle, Sir Francis Monte- fibre, Grant Allen, E. W. Hornung, Dorothy Hardy, and others, altogether forming a budget of varied and excellent literature. (Price is.) —The "Picture .Magazine"for December contains as a novel feature, a prize of .C 5 ss. and a complete set of volumes of the Picture Magazine, for the best picture solution of a puzzle. 'LIFER AND SON.—Undoubtedly the best of all the Christmas publicetions which have come to hand, is the exquisite Christmas number of " Illustrated Modern Art and. Literature' with its eight artistic coloured plates and other literary and artistic con- tents. What first draws the attention on opening the magazine is a superb colour printing on a gold background, entitled," Christians awake ! Salute the Happy Morn," from the painting by E. Eroli. It is representative of a girl in an attitude ,of ex- pressive adoration,with splendid outline and relief. "Don't tell anyone." by M. Wunech, is cer- tainly the next best picture, its chief feature being the marvellous reality of expression in the faces of the two children, one of which, with an important air, is telling the other a weighty secret and apparently impressing him profoundly with its importance and -weightuess. The other pictures are also above the average but do not come up to the last two in the exquisitemess of the expressions, but em', "Univited Guests," by G. Chierici is Pxtremely aniueing and expressive of a typical Christmas calamity. BRITISH CYCLE MANUFACTURING CO.—This firm have supplied us with their new "Ajax Cycle Catalogue for 1895. Up-to-date machines of the highest class are shown in clearly executed illus- trations, with one or two ideas for a good ladies' cycling dress, Tyres, fittings and other accessories also have a reasonable space devoted to them. It may be mentioned that this firm are at present exhibiting a large number ot machines at the Natione I Cycle Show, Crystal Palace, London. A Naas' MASS,—We have received a copy of the mass of "St. Mary Magdalen.'" in C, for voices only, for Lent and Advent, composed by the Rev. 3. E. Turner, 0..8., of War- rington. The words and order of the mass follow established lice, the opening number, Kyrie Eleison, immediately obtaining attention by reason of its powerful and devotional qualities. The , " Gloria" contains melodious choral writing, and solos for bass and tenor, which remain prominent after the chorus re-enters, and excellent effects are secured. Towards the end of the " Gloria," on the words " Cum Sancto Spirit la in Gloria. Dei Petri:4," the writing takes a fugal farm, and amply atte-te the skill of the writer. The " Credo" contains scholarly work, and on the words" Et incarnatus" • the voice writing is solemn and beautiful, and is thrown into prominence by the purposeful and studiously plain and simple organ accompaniment supplied. The "Sanctus" a piece of massive and impressive work, and world sound better if the forces employed upon it were larger and broader. The" Agnus Del" is solemn and devotional in effect, as well as rich from a merely musical point of view. Father Turner's mass is devotional and musically beautiful, and he gets his effects so simply that almost any choir might attack it with success, and he is to be congratulated upon adding to Church music a compneition in which are blended devotional feeling, melodic charm, and scholastic . writing. WARD. LOCK, AND BOWDEN, LIMITED.—Prom these publishers we have received a new "monthly" which we hive great pleasure in introducing to the general public. In construction it is somewhat eimilar to the " Strand" anil goes by the mime of '" The Windsor Magazine," and presents its first appearance in a caocelates arid tinted green cover inaugural number is dated for Jana area 1895, and with it is presented a large coloured plate entitled " Ttie Four Generetione " and representing the Queen and the infant Prince, the Duke of York and Prince of Wales. As the publishers announce, the dominant note of the magazine will be buoyant and judging from the appearance and general attractiveness of the first number,eucn a statement is likely to be verified. Two first-cless serial stories are commenced, entitled "A Bid for Fortune," by Mr. Guy Boothby, the clever fiction writer, and "The Gray Lady " from the prolific pen of Mr. Henry S. Merriman. An article which will interest all people is "Cycling as a Pursuit " by F. W.Shor- land, the well-known professional, and another is the popular "Chronicles of Martin Hewitt, Investi- gator," which have reverted from the Strand to the new periodical. The other contents which have been carefully and judiciously selected and intro- duced are "Portraite of Notable People,"Unknown. London," a comic page," What our Sisters should Wear" for the ladies,and a host of complete stories of a character which will undoubtedly cleirn the attention, and interest people of all descriptions. The general tone of the magazine is exci-•llent while the letterpress and illustrations most certainly ful- fil all desires and expectations. Last but not least of this edition's praiseworthy characteristics is its cheapness, the price being GI

CON FIRMATION BY TWO NEWS-

Beyond question, so far as the most stringent investi gation and the fullest evidence can go, is a startling occurrence jointly investigated in the public interest by two important newspapers, the " Dewsbury Chrinicle " and the " Batley Chronicle." The full name and address of the person concerned are given—Mr. Job Rice, of High-street, Hanging Beaton, near Dewsburj —and a personal interview with him is described. An apparently muscular man, of vvell_ developed physique, Mr. Race discovered one day, some three or four mouths ago,that he had put a burden upon his muscles which they would not bear. He lifted a heavy weight, felt an acute pain in his back, and found himself powerless. He had to go home, and for a long period he lay on a bed of hopeless suffering, which defied the best skill of an able doctor, who was at once summoned. Mr. Race's pain never left him. The first week lie could eat nothing. The dull, dead, heavy load of pain fixed itself in the bottom. of his back, and refused to shift. He could get no rest, nor sleep. One day he took up his copy of the "Leeds Times," and there he saw with his own eyes a description of one who had been a severe sufferer from an incurable disorder, had taken Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People, and had been miraculously cured. This was his opportunity and he seizNl it. He was a new man ere he had taken the second box. The effect was magical. Be has now had about five boxes, and is able to work as well as before the accident which paralysed him. Nothing could be more convincing than this testimony. div.head: COMPLIMENTARY DINNER AT RUNCORN TO MR. S. TAYLOR, J.P.
div.p: COMPLIMENTARY DINNER AT RUNCORN TO MR. S. TAYLOR, J.P.
INTERESTING SPEECHES.

and if thc rates were high it was not an inducement for them to come there and erect works. He thought they , compared favourably, regarding financial matters, with other towns of equal size. The speaker afterwards re- ferred m eulogistic terms to Mr. Taylor, and hoped they would carry out the spirit of the letter of the new law which had been entrusted to them. Mr. Fisher proposed the health of Mr. Pritchard (chairman of the General Purposes Committee), :trad said he had known Mr. Pritchard and worked with him for a great number of years. He had been a member of the Finance and General Purposes Commitia-e for a number of years, and he had always found Mr. Prit- chard most anxious to do everything that would be to the benefit of Runcorn. He thought had it not been for Mr. Pritchard being on the Parliamentary Committee they would not have got throueh the business with the Ship Canal Company as well as they had done. They kad several journeys to London, and he was sur n that the way Mr. Pritchard acquitted himself there was a credit to Runcorn. He hoped Mr. Pritchard would be returned again to take a prominent part on the new council. Mr. Pritchard said he had certainly been a member of the Parliamentary Committee since it had been estab- lished, and had an excellent training in the very diffi- cult questions which early came under its notice, by the construction of the Manchester Ship Canal. It was part of their duty to see where that great undertaking touched the intert.sts of Runcorn. It was their duty to study the bearings of the construction of that canal on Runcorn, and provide clauses that would protect their drainage system, protect the trade on the river, and also the other important interests which were affected through the construction of that great work. He Wad never heard it brought to the charge of that committee that they neglected their duties. They had had to I manage the important question of taking over the water works and getting the parliamentary powers necessary. The committee had now charge of the most impertant question of a graving dock and the arrangemen,s with the Canal Company. He trusted that they might be successful in coming to some satisfactory arrangement in this matter. With regard to the Board of Commis- sioners it had been in existence 42 years. The speaker afterwards referred to a number of new Acts which had been imnosed upon the Commissioners and which en- tailed a laTge accession of work to the duties of the Com- missioners in recent years. These had caused an amount of expenditure, as would be seen from the fact, that, whereas the rate was is. Bd. about 10 or 12 years ago, it was now 2,.10d. in the £. They could only hope that when this new authority was formed, it would take up and carry on this work which tQ the present time had been carried on fairly successfully by the Board of Commissioners. - - - - - -

Mr. Bisbrown in proposing the health of Mr. Imison (chairman of the Health Committee) said Mr. Imison, owing to his position as chairman touched at times cer- tain interests, hut it was to his credit, that he acted with the utmost impartiality. Ha dealt out justice to every person. Referring to the trade depression, the speaker said he thought one of the causes which had brought it about were the American tariffs. But with the New Year he was of the opinion that there vinu'd be a decided improvement in trade. For some months now the managers had been accumulating very heavy stocks and they had got to such a pitch that the directors had felt it their duty to clear out their stocks. The speaker also referred to the Board of Commissioners, mentioning a number of worthy members who were now deceased. Mr. Imison responded to the toast, and in referring to the work of the Health Committee, said unless the I Board were in sympathy with the work the committee I had in hand, its recommendations could not be carried out and consequently improvements could not be made. Speaking of Mr. Taylor, he said he had had the honour and privilege of serving with him in four different capacities, and in every one of them he would like to beer testimony to the very excellent and capable way Mr. Taylor had done his duties. He had been more in- timately connected with him as officer. He had always found him most helpful and most sincerely anxious to do his duty. He was exceedingly sorry that Mr.Hand- ley had withdrawn his candidature from the new Coun- cil. He had distinguished himself as a member of the Board, and was there long before he (the speaker) was. He hoped that Mr. Handley would again sit round the table in the Boardroom. He should like to see some of the old members returned. He (Mr. Imison) had been a member of the Board eight years, and he could say that every member of the Board had been animated by one desire,and that was the general prosperity of the town. (Applause.) Mr. Abel proposed the toast of the health of the Chairman of the Canal Boats and Markets Committee (Mr. Flankinson). He thought Mr. Hankireion had done his duty in every respect, and he was very sorry to hear that he was to retire from their midst. He saw that some of the candidates for the new council were raising a cry abeut the canal boats, and casting a slur upon the committee. He did not know of a single complaint that had been made to the committee about any canal boat which had not been dealt with fairly. He thought the officiate bed performed their duties satisfactorily, and he considered that no board had done better work than the present Board of Commissioners. Mr. Flankinson replied to the toast, and said he had still the same good feeling towards his brother commis- sioners, although he had turned his hack on them, in a sense, by not seeking, re-election. He would like to see the matter of a vehicular bridge across the Mersey pushed forward. They were at a disadvantage in Run- corn in only having one entrance into the town. He hoped the fawn would become a market town, although shopkeepers were onpoeed to it. He thought it would increase the trade of Runcorn to have a good market With regard to the canal boats it had been drummed into his ears that certain leniency had been shown tr. some members of the Beard in this matter. He defied any person to come forward and show that any official had not faithfully discharged his duties. Those persons who had been reported before the committee had been brought to book. He had tried to do his duty irrespec- tive of persons, and the officials of the Beard had won the respect of et ery commissioner. (Applause.) Mr. Grice in proposing the health of Mr. Handley (chairman of the Library Cemmittee), remarked that he was very sorry to find that Mr. Handley had retired from seeking re-election on the district council. He was certain that as Chairman of the Library Committee. Mr. Handley had taken a deep interest in the welfare of the people of Runcorn. He was never more at home than when catering for the public—books, and for the intelli- gence of the people. He hoped that at some tarty data they would see him a number of the Distriet Council. He -hoped also to see a number of his old colleagues elected to the new council.

The members and officials of the Runcoen Board of Commissioners gave a complimentary dinner to the Chairman of the Board (Mr. S. Taylor, J.P.) at Wilson's Hotel, Runcorn, on Friday evening. There were present in addition to Mr. Taylor' Messrs. F. Wiswall, J. Prit- chard, J. Mea.dowerr:ft, W. Handley, R. Abel, J. W. Lightburn' W. Fisher, D. Bisbrown, E. Imieon, W. Collier, H.J. Grice, W. Hankinson, J. B. Holland, F. A. Lake (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), M. Barker (surveyor), J. Wilding (assistant surveyer), and W. Jones (.collector). After the dinner which was served in Mr. Dutton's best style, the Chairman (Mr. Wiswall) proposed the toast of "The Queen and the members of the Royal family," which was drunk with enthusiasm. Mr. Wis. , wall in proposing the health o Mr. S. Taylor said it was the most important toast of the evening. It was Mr. Meadowcroft who suggested that that complimentary dinner should take place, and the members of the Board readily fell in with the suggestion. Whether they looked upon 'Mr. Taylor as a youth, a husband, a public man, a magistrate, or as a master, he presented the most admirable features. If they had more of his type in the country he was sure they would have more prosperous times and less of the unemployed. This question of the unemployed presented one of the most difficult problems that needed solution. How that problem was to be solved he could not tell. At any rate they knew that the Chairman of their Board had an interest in the town, and took an interest in the Board in every branch, and every feature of its business and everything pertaining to its prosperity. (Applause.) After the drinking of the toast the audience sang "For he's a jolly good fellow." Mr. Taylor responding said he accepted the invitation which he received from them gth the greatest . pleasure. He was very grate- AOl ta them for their kindness in inviting him there that night. He had occupied the position of chair- man of the board about eighteen months, and he was sure no chairman could have had a more pleasant time than he had bad with the gentlemen on the board he had worked with. He was sure it had been the desire of every member, not to harass each other, but to give to the utmost of their ability the attention which the interests of the tewn had required. He had been on the board semething near 20 years and he must say that during the last three or four years he had in his experience, never passed so pleasant a time. The desire of every member had been for the welfare of the town. He had, during his time, sat on the board when there had been friction very much greater than during the last three or four years. Of course they must always expectewhere there were 18 members sitting on a board, that they could not all look at things with one eye. But he thonght it would be woe to any town where they had a happy family of that mind. Every man was entitled to have an opinion of his own, and he would not think very much of any man who had not one. Dur- ing the time he had been chairman of the board his experience was that every member had expressed his opinion fearlessly, and he must say they had always agreed to differ and as long as that was the case there was no fear of any dangerous results. They had had many important questions before them, and had it not been for the thoughtful considerations given to tile3' questions by the members, Runcorn would not have been in so good a position as it was to-day. (Applause). He referred particularly to the Ship Canal during the time of its construction. They had their sewage scheme and ether matters which they settled amicably and left a good feeling on both sides at the conclusion of the negotiations. They might, considering their position on the banks of the canal, had they not been careful, been thrown into serious lawsuits with the Com- pany. But he must say that with the careful considera- tion of every member they had kept clear of any disputes. They were now drawing near to the termination of the old Board of Commissioners, but he hoped that the new council, whoever its members might be, would work to the great advantage of the town as the past Board of Commissioners ha') dene. (Applause). In proposing the toast of" the town and trade of Runcorn," Mr. Wiswell said trade seemed to be in a depressed etate just now, but they must hope for better time. It, was not the first time trade had been de- pressed and that gave them hope for the future. He was sure that the gentlemen present were all more or less interested in the trade and prosperity of the town. It was unfortunate that at the close of their Board of Commissioners, trate was in a depregsed staee. He thought they left a good record behind them. (Applause.) Ho would couple with the toast the name of Mr. Hol- land. Mr. Holland of Parr's Banking Company said the company he was connected with were greatly interesel in the trade and prosperity of the town. There was not the slightest doubt that the country was going through a time of great depression in trade, Perphaps it. was only natural that while the Ship Canal was being made there was brought, into the town a great amount o money which now had-ceased to pass. Tnat wee inund to affect every trade in Runcorn. Beyond that there was, unfortunately, a depression in the Alkali trade. Many men lied been stopped and working expenditure was 'being reduced all through. How lon g that woold lai,t he did not know. But. he thought there was a silver lining to the cloud. Runcorn was ntturalle the port on the Ship Canal. They had got two ways into it, and to enter it ships were not required to drop their masts as there were no bridges to pass. Manchester fit,Plllevi to think that everything should go there, and Runcorn was paying the penalty at the present tima. But he was confident that Manchester and every port along the hanks of the canal -would eventually be worked for what it could do. Let them eive i t time and it would cerne. Referring to Mr. Taylor he said lie was the gentle- man, they had come to honour that night, and he did in sonic measure represent the town and trade of Runcorn. Since he (Mr. Holland) had been in Runcorn he had met Mr. Taylor in many capacities, in private, public and:in busieess and taking tom, all in all, they would not meet with hie like again. (Applause.) Mr. W. Collier proposed the health of the Chairman of the Finance Committee (Mr. Lighthurn), and said the v all knew what a magic word finance was. It ruled the roast. Finance must have a very sound constitution, and he did not. think their chairman ef the Finance Committee looked like a falling currency. (Laughter.) He helmet Mr. I.eghtburn would be returned for his ward with a handsome majority. it was of the greatest im- portance that they should get this committee right. It did not matter much about the others. (Laughter.) They had all to come to this melting pot. (Renewed laughter.) Mr. Liehtburn, in responding, said he thought the Finance Committee had perhaps less to do than some people imagined because every committee was in itself a spending one, altho ugh the expenditure came before the Finance Committee. He said they heard talk about baths,free recreation grounds, and other matters, which everyone of them would like to see established in Run- corn. But it must be remembered that the trade of the town depended upon the taxes of the piece. When any- one came to Runcorn with a view to opening works one the first questions was " what taxes have you got 9'
I with the greatest

- Mr. Handley said it was with feelings of regret that.he had decided through circumstances over which he bad no control, and which he stated to Mr. Lake at the time of his refusal, not to seers election on the district coun- cil. It had always given him pleasure to do any work for the Board of Commissioners, but he did not think that it would be the last time he would sit round that table." (Hear, hear.) It was about the sear 1876 when he was first elected on the Board and he cootinued until 1885 when there were certain reasons why he should retire. Although he was elected, he was prevented from taking his seat. Some of them would recollect when he again became a member of the Board. tie thanked them heartily for having recognised his services on the ILibrary Committee. It was one of the red letter days in his life when in 1882, the free library Was- opened. There was another work which had been placed in their hands and that was the Technical Institute. In connec- tion with that no one had worked harder than Mr. Wis- wall. He believed Mr. Wiswall owed his present posi- tion to technical instruction, and there was no wonder that he took such a deep interest in the work of the in- stitute. He hoped it would be put to the use for which it was intended. He proposed the health of Mr. Wis- wall. (Applause.) Mr. Wiswall in thanking the members for the toast said-some people thought that the matter of technical instruction in Runcorn was a fad of his. But the Board 1 by vote undertook to adopt the act, and add a penny Irate for that object. They had now got a .teohnical i 13- stitute in the town and it was for the new council to work it. He was very glad that the working classes were taking such a considerable interest in the matter, and no ow+ was more pleased to know, that the men for whom it was intended were going to patrc,nrize and use it. , • Mr. Taylor proposed the health of the Chairman of the Water Committee (Mr. Meadowcrott). In doing so lie said he thought that the purchase of that undertaking by the Board was the greatest undertaking they had en. gaged in. There was a great deal of contention, and A great deal said about it at the time, which . was mot at all pleasant to some of them. But he was delighted to find that after twelve month's experience, they had a surplus of £5OO. No member of their board took a greater interest in the matter, frOm the very commence- ment, than Mr. Meadowcroft, and he was truly sorry that he had seen his way to leave the Board. Mr. Meadowcrolt said he was extremely pleased that the first twelve month's working of the water works had been so satisfactory, and he trusted that in the future they would find no greater difficulty than they had done in the past.. The water works were turned over to them in good working order, and thus they incurred no in- cidental expenditure. But in the rmure he thought they must be prepared for some anxiety and perhaps a littli more difficulty. There would he the question of water supply. They were, however, in the fortunate position of being able to get a supply of Vynrwy water at a moderate price. Be hoped that the new authority would work with the same good spirit and with the same single • purpose as the old members. Mr. Wiswall proposed the health of the " Press," and this svas suitably respoluled to. The Chairman also pro- posed the health of the officers of the Board. He was sure there was no town in the country with a better staff of c fiieers. He thought the services of their Surveyor (Mr. Barker) were unique, he having :q,rveit them for 41 years.—Mr. Barker, in responding, said there were only \ two of their commissioners living who were on the Board when he was appointed snrveyors—Mr. Lake, (law i eleik), and Mr. Marshall (cecretary), also briefly re- sponded to the toast. . During the evening sons were contributed by Mr. E. pillion, aria Mr. J. VV. Isighasur.

'IEEE I.4INANIINER9 SATURDAY DECEMBER 15 1894.-. TIME TA BLE PROPERTY DISPUTE AT WARRINGTON. RAILWAY CARLISLE v. MESSRS. BISHOP AND COMPANY. At the Lancashire Chancery Court, St. George's Hall, DECEMBER • Liverpool,n Wednesday last week.befort. Vice-Chaucel- tor Robinson, an ar;tion was brought by Mr. Frederick Johc Carlisle, the owner of seven cottages in Dial-court, Cockhedge-lane, Warrington, against Messrs. W. Bishop and Company, the owners of some adjoining pr3perty, for an injunction to restrain them from obstructing his right of way and his ancient lightq,and from trespassing on his premises. Mr. Rotch and Mr. Cunningham appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Laurence and Mr. Hughes for the defendants. The plaintiff's case was that the defendants had recently pulled down some cottages at the back of plaintiff's property, and plocceded to erect a large building, the wail of which came close to the back of plaintiff's cottages, actually over his boundary line, completely blocking an ancient right of way at the back into Cockhedge-lane, damaging his ancient lights and interfering with his drainage.—The defence was a general denial of interference with plaintiff's legal ' rights. The hearing was adjourned.
