div.head: IMPORTANT PROPERTY SALE AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: IMPORTANT PROPERTY SALE AT WARRINGTON.

One of the most important property sales ever held in the recollection of Warrington people took place at the Lion Hotel, Warrington, on Wednes- day last week. Between 300 and 400 of the leading people of Warrington and dis- trict were present and the lots went off well. A. remarkable fact in connection with the sale was that the whole 47 lots were sold, which is almost unprecedented in sales of this nature. The following were the most important lots and the prices at which they were sold. A freehold farm in Cross-lane, Appleton, with house and outbuildings, and a freehold cottage and garden, in all containing ata. 3r. 21p. was sold for £1,600. Two freehold dwelling- houses and several fields in Cross-lane, Apple- ton, containing 16a. Or. 22p., £1,375. A freehold dwelling-house in Red-lane, Apple- ton. with freehold cottage and a portion of a field, £l,lOO. A freehold plot of building land in Red-lane, Appleton, and a freehold field containing Ba. ir. 7fp. £1,300. Two freehold fields at Wools- ton, £1,005. A freehold farm, Brookhouse farm at Orford, containing 14a. Or. 17p. £1,020, A freehold freehold beerhouse—the "Limerick," at Burton- wood, .£BOO. A freehold farm, known as Smithy House farm, at Burtonwood, con- taining 155 acres, £7,300. " Critchley's Farm' at Burtonwood, containing 64 acres, £2,375. Higher Joy-lane farm, Burtonwood, 26 acres, £975. A drapers shop, 4, Buttermar- ket-atreet, Warrington' and warehouse and por- tion of site of cottage £1,450. Amongst the other lots were included 49 Parr's Bank shares all of which realised between £76 103. and .£77 per share. Eight Warrington Corporation perpetual gas annuities of £2 each brought £535. A large num- ber of Warrington Corporation redeemable gas annuities were also sold for good prices.

div.head: TITE WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY'S
div.p: TITE WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY'S

CONCERT. On Tuesday evening last week the first of two Chamber Concerts which com- prise the Warrington Nlusical Society's programme for the present season was given in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-sr— beforf; a fashionable audience which comfortably filled the room. By force of circumstances the members of the Society's chorus and orchestra are prevented from giving their customary concerts en masse, though good work .in pursuing the objects of the society is still being done by the continuance, as usual, of the members' weekly meetings for practice. Although given under the society's auspices the concert under notice is really the outcome of private effort put forth by Mr. F. H. Crossley the society's conductor, and Mr. F. W. Reynolds, with the double object of preserving a continuity of touch between the Musical Society and the public, and of raising funds to be devoted to reducing an adverse balance incurred by the Society during two recent unfortunate seasons. For the excellent concert of Tuesday evening and the money surplu3 which may he expected to result from it, the Society must, therefore, feel its indebt- edness to the two gentlemen named, whose gratis services formed so important an element in the programme. Messrs. Crossley and Reynolds as violinist and pianist, respectively. Mr. Carl Fuchs as 'cellist, and Madame Dews as vocalist, took upon themselves the whole burden of the concert, and, to the lover of the " classical" in music, they were all-sufficient The trios for piano and strings which opened and closed the programme were somewhat tediously long, and the suggestion may be pardoned that a couple of movements only in each instance, selected from similar compositions of greater intrinsic interest, would have proved more acceptable to the audience. Neither the C minor op. 1 No. 3 Beethoven, nor the trio in F by Gade, represent what is most effective and pleasing in concerted muGic of this character. Of Mr. Crosslev's violin soles the best were undoubtedly' the " Bolero " is E. German) and the " Cavatina ' (Raff) which he played in re!,ponse to a recall; and in these Mr. Crossley gave evidence of taste and executive ability of no mean order. As a 'cellist Mr. Carl Fuchs has long since established himself in the good opinion of Warrington audiences, and it will suffice to Gay that alike in the quaint old-worldli- ness of Perpora's Sonata, and in the charming piquantness of Popper's present-time moreeauz,llerr Fuchs delighted his hearers with that intelligent interpretation of the composers' meaning, and that masterly command of the resources of his instru- ment which characterise all his performances. Mr. Reynold's pianoforte solos were, as might be expected, well chosen and skilfully performed. The Romance in B flat (Rubinstein) is in the com- poser's more subdued and tranquil vein, and its performance may he regarded as a graceful tribute to the memory of a recently departed genius. In Mr. Reynolds interpretation of both this and the " Valse brilliante " of Moszowski, there was notice- able an exquisite touch coupled with a reserve of power which was always artistically because intel- ligently displayed. Madame Dews gave pleasant vaciety to the programme by her rendering of " The Three Fishers" (Hullah), and of the new song "Rest." to which Mr. Crossley played a violin obligato. Although adaptations are, as a rule, dis- appointing and unworthy, this version of Handel's well-known" Largo" is so far an exception that Madame Dews was able to impart to it an effective- ness and a pathos bath real and artistic. Madame Dews possesses, however, the rare faculty of self- abandonment which, coupled with a rich voice, al- ways ensures a large degree of success in a ' vocalist. The song " The Weaver's Dream "(Moir) was conspicuously devoid of merit in both words and music, and it is not surprising therefore that it failed to engage the serious attention of the audience. A concert grand pianoforte (Kaps) sup- plied by Mr. Pearson was used. DESECRATION OF NATURE. Although the Homocea Co. have had one of the greatest schemes in rural advertising put before them, they have declined to entertain it on account of the widespread disgust existing in the minds of all who love their woods, dales, fields, streams, rocks and hills in the glory of their natural beauties, undefiled by the modern billposter. They (The Homocea Co.), are content with the legitimate channel of the Press, and by Pamphlets containing Testimonials. They can point to cures, far more convincing than mere assertion. PANTOMIME AT ST. JAMES' SCHOOL.
"THE FOUR SEASONS."

The large room ot St. James' Schools was crowded on Monday evening,when "The Four Seasons "represented by the same number of young ladies as daughters of Father Time, were enacted in a pantomime. In the pantomime the four seasons are supposed to be married to the four quarters amid joyful festivities. The follow- ing are the characters and their imparsonators :—Father Time, Mr. W. H. Stansfield ; Spring, Miss Ditchfie!d ; first quarter, Mr. Acton ; Summer, Miss Sutton ; second quarter, Mr. A. Thornley ; Autumn, Miss Webb ; third quarter, Mr. J. Millewood ; Winter,Miss Wright ; fourth quarter, Mr. J. H. Warburton. Tuere were also four maids of honour viz. :—Misses Gladys Adams, Madge Davies, Doris Adams, and Dora Millewood ; four pages : Masters Gilbert Slater, S. Burgess, E. Gordon Burgess, and Herbert MillewoOd. No pantomime being complete without a clown, a very excellent one was provided in the person of Mr. J. Wood. The traditional sweep was also enrolled, being personated in a successful manner by Mr. David Green. Mr. Millewood was a great success as cheap-jack and the harvestman was ably represented by Mr. Litton. Other characters were Father Christmas, Mr. Caldwell, and nigger, Mr. Dowling. The Misses Reynolds and Masters A. Newton and W. Tuft, were deservedly successful in pleasing the audience in the hornpipe dance while the former young ladies further contributed to the evening's enjoyment by a clever skirt dance. An encore was demanded and re- sponded to for both these performanees. Mr. Frank Booth was the accompanist. The wigs, &c., were sup- plied by Mr. Birch Brown, and the scenery was specially painted by Mr. F. J. Dell. A clever representation of "The Old Feathers Inn," Ludlow, was portrayed on the exterior scenery together with Stokesay Castle in the distance, while the interior scenery shows the inside of" The Feathers Inn." The limelight was thrown on the scenes by Messrs. H. M. Houghton and Cuthbert Slater. Father Time commenced the proceedings of the , pantomime with a descriptive prologue. The songs were all characteristic of the different parts and people included in the prop...ramine'and were greatly appreciated by the audience. Morris and maypole dances, shep- herdesses, haymakers, reapers, ac., were pleasingly re- presented by children, and their varied dances and per. formances were very gracefully executed. The maypole dance was also performed in very good time, and the many coloured bands winding round the pole gave addi- tional brightness to the scene. Frequent bursts of ap- plauso testified to the success of the pantomime,and the persons who had the training of the children and other performers in hand,are entitled to warm congratulation. On Tuesday and Wednesday evenings the pantomime was further continued, and the first night's success was well sustained.

div.head: PLAYING GAMES OF CHANCE.
div.p: PLAYING GAMES OF CHANCE.
PROSECUTIONS AT WARRINGTON.

At the Borough Police Court on Monday morning, Thomas Higgs, boilermaker, 46, Queen-st., and Joseph Price, warehouseman, Queen-eteet, were charged with having on Saturday last, Bth December, unlawfully played a game of chance, called" Spinning Jenny" on the open ground off Church-st.—Mr. Hunt (chief con- stable) said there was a sort of " fair" going on at Howley Quay near Ellesmere-St. schocls and on Satur- day night list P.C.'s Corbett and Barnett were on duty there and about seven o'clock informed Inspector Spinks ef having seen the defendants playing a game of chance by means of a marked board with a spinning finger in the middle. People put their money on the colours and the person whose snoney the finger stopped at was en- titled to a silk handkerchief. Higgs had paid toll for the stand of his paraphernalia. Inspector Spinks said that he saw the game in full motion with coins on each colour and the handkerchiefs all round. The first de- fendant was shouting " Now's your time ! Pick your colour ! Pick your colour !" and the next defendant was taking the money and otherwise aiding and abetting. Twenty persons could deposit their pennies but only one win and when the finger stopped at a blank space the defenlants raked all the money in. The officers brought the defendants and their " machine" to the police s'ation and found over £4 tipon Higgs, much of which was in copper. P.C.'s Barnett, Corbett, Foster, and Sergeant Rowbothans all spoke to seeing the defendants manipulating the gaming table and receiving money. Mr. Place, market inspector, deposed to taking the defend- ant's toll, but he had not noticed the game. He would not have allowed them to stand if he had caught them playing an illegal game. Both defendants had boen ad- mitted to bail. Higgs was fined £1 and costs and Price ss. and costs, with the forfeiture of the gaming table. Their defence was ignorance of wrong-doing. Elizabeth Ambrose, no settled abode, was charged with playing the same game for a toffee prize at the same place on Saturday. P.C.'s Barnett and Corbett proved seeing the woman playing this game with toffee and cocoa-nuts as prizes. On seeing the officers she stopped but on them moving away recommenced. On being anprehended the woman had said that she paid toll to Mr. Place who had said there was no harm in the game. Mr. Place denied having said this. Mr. Hunt said that the toffee was not fit for eat- ing. On consideration of defendant's large family a fine of ss. and costs only was imposed and the materials for the game forfeited.

div.head: T iiE EX A MINE R
div.p: T iiE EX A MINE R
SATURrLY, DECEMBER 15, 1834.

THE South of England does not The Premier cri seem to be favourable to the Politics. growth of Liberalism, but that there are Liberals in that part of tho country, and many of them, was testified by the remarkable meeting which Lord •RaSpERY addressed at IDevonport on Tuesday, and by the crowds which .gathered at railway stations to give him. .a cheering word. The Premier made . an excellent speech. He is not cast down by the :result of the recent 'bye-elections in Forfar and at Brigg. :Bye-elec- tions, as an almost invariable rule, go against the party in power. The only difference betwem the experiences of the present Government and thoH3 of its Tory .predecessors, is that the latter .were particularly unfortunate .in the matter o• .elections while the former have so far been un- usually fortunate. In the first two years of tie existence of the late •Government no fewer than eleven seats were transferred from them to the Opposition.; in the two year's tenure of office of the present Government only four seats have been lost, three of them at the polls and one by defec- tion. This leaveaa very fair balance to the, credit of the present Government. It would have been mere satisfactory, of course, if both Forfar and Brigg had been retained. lEiiat the Opposition, like other Oppositions, .are entitled to :their crumbs of comfort. They have :found that 'when they are blessed with strong :local candidates and backed up by a solid philla.nx.of plural voters they can occasionally min a seat. The result of the two elections does not justify any more definite conclusion than that. At a .general election,••for instance, the plural voter cannatbewhipped up so easily, and the electoral success which is won ,by his help at a bye-election may !be lost when he is fully engaged nearer home. Liberals do not loa upon either Forfar or Brigg Hs finally transferred to the Tories. Lord ROSEI3ERY also dealt in ar.: effective manner with the remarkable statement: of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN that "no working man is the; richer, the wiser, or the happier fer.all the labours of the Gladstonite Government." This utterance of the Birmingham politician isespeeiallyludicrous at the present time. Al! over the rural parts of En land and Wales workingmen havejust been given a voice in the management QS their local . affairs such as they have never had before. If this „does not make them happier they have Jost the .love of self-government which has madeothis cone- try what it is. And,if it .does not in the end make tleeen richer—that is to say, ireptee.;e their eaat( rich condition—they will have themselves to bleme . The clairee made by Mr. CIL:t.,M3ER- 11,A$A- tconlil sound especially ludicrous in be ,part thoreonetry where Lord Pommel, was speAaing. The man employed in the Itlyal dockyards have T.-ease-etc-, acknowndge that their lot has 1-4eeti ievrovecl by the present Government. As Lord RoZitIBBfAY took occasion to point out, some .1.4,1kYJ men have had their hours of labour reduced froaa nearlyfifty-two to forty-eight a week, while sortie £3O On year had been added to their wageael Under the'Wer Department -19,000 more workmera. have siecilerlv•benefitted, while, as regards work- d men at age, the influence of the Government aa a model employer must be of a car-re-aching char- acter. Lor4.:ROSl3l4Enr was also fully entitled to claim credit for tharesults of a Liberal administra- tion in Ireland. By canoting the Judges who have held Assize e in various parts, of Ireland he was :able to show that that country is enjoying a eingular immtmity from ea:imes of an agrarian or Ipelitical character, That ia not a result cf eeer- cion : it is a proof of the vctiedom of the Liberal policy in dispensing with coereio-. A year Or eo ego Afr. Moerze was strongly aged by his Tory crities to have recourse t that fevonrite reeled y of thrs, exceptional legialatiow; hut he firmly declined the specious but not disieterest ed invita- tion ; and irelyeis Lord ItoseeneY feed, he has his 'reward in 0a centente.d end yreepereur Leland." No political speech is complete • at the present time without a referenc to the House of Lords, and the Premier's remarks on this great ques- tion seem to have been received with peculiar gratification by his audience. It is now quite clear that the Government is thoroughly in bar- :h.. -12_1t ;

on this subject. It does not intend to strengthen the House of Lords under the plea of reform. Its one object is to make the House of Commons supreme. "We are," says Lord ROIEMIERY, "determined, if the power be given us by the country, so to limit and circumscribe the powers of mischief and mutilation possessed by the House of Lords that we shall have little or nothing to dread from that power in the futura."

THE reports of the Parish Council Parish Meetings. meetings which have been made . public from various parts of th e • country are "variegated," to say the least. There have been model meetings, and other meetings that have been conducted in a way which offers nothing that is worthy of iknitation. In some , parts of the country the parsons have been a good deal in request as chairmen • and in other ways in other parts they have scarcely been looked at. In this district several Church of .England clergymen have offered their services as, • councillors, but in quite a notable number f stances their .services have been declined. The number of votes given have generally just fallen short of what was requisite to placethem amongst the successful candidates. At some meetings— though not in this neighbourhood—peers and baronets have presided; in some • few instance s labourers have been elected to thepost of dignity, and the 'village schoolmaster ,has often been called uponito fill the breach. An extraordinary•case is reported from •Cambridgcshire of a clergyman dis- chargiug the schoolmaster for calling him to order from the chair at a parish meeting. Tnis is an interference with the liberty of .the subject that needs looking into, and it is to be hoped that this intolerant clergyman will be called to account. The meeting places have been as varied as the chairmen. In the vast majority of cases the meetings have,of.course, been held in the village schoolroom, but there are instances of their being held in the Church and even in the Wesleyan Chapel. There seems to be a pretty unanimous dislike to the method of vot- inglat parish meetings—that is to say, by an open slow of hands. Labourers, and others who are not labourers, have of tenielt that they could not vote in this way as they should like to vote. A story is told that at one meeting when the squire's name was put there was at °first but a very .poor show of hands, but when the •squire rose to his feet and fixed his gaze upon the back seats. where the labourers of the village were,quite a number of "horny hands" were suddenly held up. The system of 'voting at parish meetings • should be altered. It does not conduce to a fall and honest , expression • of opinion.

—; • VOLUNTEER. INTELLIGENCE. Tuesday night's " London CiruZ,Lte " contained the following with reference to the 2nd (Earl of Chester's) Volunteer Battalion Cheshire Regiment: —" Major -Fluitt, retired, is re-appointed to the battalion as captain, and is granted the honorary rank of major." "Ova ANCESTORS AND THEIR RELIGION." This was the subject of a lecture given by Mr. G. Bowyer, of Runcorn, in connection with the Bible and Mutual Improvement Class at Weston on Mo day evening. Air. S. Dodd presided, and there was a good attendance. BRUNSWICK-ST-lEET WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS. At the usual weekly meeting of this chi's at Runcorn on Tuesday evening, Miss Clayton, L.L.A. gave an interesting paper on " Some Aspect's ot Modern Litera',ure." The chair was occupied by Mr. T. Simister, and there was a fair attendance of members. A short discussion followed the reading of the paper. BETHESDA. LITERARY AND SOCIAL CLASS. RuNCORN. At the meeting of this class on Tuesday evening, the Rev.. J. Simpson continued his course of - lectures on Tennyson. He gave a continuation of his subject at the previous, lecture that of" woman," as depicted in TennYson's "Princess." As beariag on the same subject, the rev, gentleman referred to the character " Lindell" in " The Story of an African Farm " by Olive Schreiner. A short dis- cussion ensued at the close of the lecture. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD_ A meeting of this board was held at the Burial Board offices on Wednesday afternoon. Mr. W. F. Salkeld, secretary, submitted a statement of accounts which showed that the interments during the eight months prior to November 25, numbered 201, and for the corresponding period last year 362, being a decrease of 161. The fees received during the same period were .El9l Os.Bd.as against i:334 188. last year, being a decrease of £143 Bs. 4d. The accsonts were passed. FonmeN MISSIONARY SERVICES AT RUNCORN. The Rev. W. George preached the foreign mision- • ary sermons in Camden Wesleyan Chapel on Sunday. The congregations Were unusually large. On ;Ni‘mday there was an interesting meeting, presided over by Mr. Edward Taylor in the absence of Mr. John Simpson. Mr. John Robinson threw some very appropriate scenes on the scrcen with his fine limelight lantern. Avery effective address was given on Ceylon, by the Rev. John Landford, ret uriaed missionary. The Rev. W. George read the local report. Collections were taken, and were nearly .E 4 in advance of last year. VISIT OF MR. POWELL THOMAS TO RUNCORN. This well-known popular lecturer, musician, and elocutionist,has been engaged to give a concert and entertainment in connection with the Bethesda Literary and Social Class on Tuesday evening in the lecture roam. The programme will include in- teresting songs,humorous, pathetic, and descriptive recitals and gems of Weigh melodies with favourite selections of English, Scotch, and Irish national airs. Mr. Thomas has paid visits to numerous Literary and Mechanics' Institutions in the:*country and his visit, may be looked forward to with Pleasure. Mr. A. R. NormanoT.R, will be the chairman. SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN. The wife of Mr. Gedrge Ernest Sherratt, of 6, Stanley-st., died suddenly on Thursday morning. The deceased who was 22 yearo of age was only married an the sth inst., her maislen name being Francis Hughes, of Sinam's Cross,Wid nes. On Sun- , day last she visited her mother-in-law,Mre.Sherratt, of 14, Albert-terrace, Runcorn, and partook of , supper .with the family. During the nig'.t she became seriously ill, and had a bilious attack on Monday. he was considerably better on Tuesday and continued so until Wednesday forenoon when she became worse. Dr. Robinson was called in and treated her for biliousness, but she died between seven and eight o'clock on Thursday morning. Tile facts have been reported to the poli2e. A 'SOCIAL GATHERING AT ,RUNCORN. A very pleasant evening was spent in the Bethesda school on Wednesday by those who re- cently took part in the rendition of the cantata at the choir services in the Congregational Church. After a capital tea, the evening was spent in a soci- able spanner. The Rev..f. Simpson delivered a brief address, in which he stated that they were indebted to Mr. Le Couteur, the organist, who gave such valuable service in the preparatinn of the cantata " The Healing of Naaman." Songs were sung by Miss Edwards, Mr. Le,athwood and Mr. Pilgrim. Various games were indulged in during the even- ing,
al UNICORN POLICE COUnT.

At this court on -Tuesday before Mr. f. J. Nor- man and 'Mr. T. Handley, an old off,mder named Mary Murphy was charged with being guilty of indecent behaviour, the previous night, and was sent to gaol for three months' hard labour. The Bench told the prisoner that if she came before them again she would he dealt with as 9,n incorrig- ible rogue.—William Knight. Prescot Terrace, was also fined 54. and costs for indecent behaviour. A SHIP COOKIS ESCAPADE ON A RUNCORN BOAT.

The Flint police have handed over to the Holy- ' head police authorities a young man named John Edwards, of Flint, apprehended on a charge of breaking into a ship's cabin, and stealing a silver watch and a quantity of money. The prisoner way cook on board the Lizzie, of Chester, owned by a Runcorn firm, and on the 21st ult. was at Holy- head. In the absence of the captain and mate, the , captain's cabin was broken into by the breaking of the skylight, and the Watch and money stolen. No clue was discovered as to the perpetrator up to Saturday last. The schooner was unloading at Runcorn and the lad got leave for a few days, and on Saturday afternoon be tendered at the pawn-' broker's establishment at Flint kept by Mr. Richard 'Williams, a silver watch.. Mr.Williams,u,fon seeing the watch, compared it with the particulars given of the watch stolen at Ffolyhead, which had been forwarded to his Bangor premises. He communi- cated with the captain of the Lizzie(William Jones, Shot ton-lane, Connah's quay), and information was subsequently given to Police-inspector Minshull, who arrested the prisoner, and detained him. He will be brought up at the Holyhead court.
BOARD SCHOOL CONCERT AND PRIZE
DIST RIBU FION AT RUNCORN.

The Runcorn Public Hall was crowded on Thursday evening when the children attending the Greenway- road Board schools provided a most enjoyable entertain- ment. Pr:zes for regular attendance and efficiency during the year were distributeci by Mr. Tomkinson in the unavoidable absence of his wife. Dr. McDougall occupied the chair, and there were also on the platform Mr.Tomkinson, Mr. Pritchard and Mr. Moss. The Chairman said before they proceeded with the evening's entertainment he had to congratulate the teachers of the Greenwar-road schools for the excellent work done there. lie had had placed in his hand by Mr. Moulton a statement which would give them a good and accurate account of the work that he and his eo-workers had done since this prize system had been established. Since the prize system was inaugrated- £6O had been collected by the method they were adopting that evening. The distribution of prizes had produced an excellent result in getting a good attendance of the children. He thought they would agree with him that it was a very important matter that the children should attend school regularly. If it was worth while sending thorn to school at all, it was worth while sending them regularly, for it was by regularity that they were likely to get on. The irregular child had often a poor chance of getting a prize unless it was poses,,.ed of above the average intellect. All the money that went in prizes was reised by voluntary effort, and not one penny came out of the rates He thought that these efforts ought to be en- couraged, and the teachers to be congratulated on thelT work. The average attendance was very encouragine. and it rested with the parents to make the attendance ere; ter. The schools at Heath-road had been very much under a cloud, but had been raised under the Board, to school of considerable importance, and at the present Vine formed a nucleus for the Greenway-road Board schools. The Board was at the present time engaged in a work which in time would come under the notice of the ratepayers, but he hoped the sting of having to increase the rates would be mollified con- siderably by the results which he thought they must agree were very satisfactory indeed. They were doing admirable work. The speaker after- wards proceeded to speak on the importance of the ap- pointment of inspectors for science and art schools. Over £2OO was received in Runcorn for technical education from the Cheshire County Council, but the method of examination and of supervision was, in his opinion, faulty, and it would he a c'ond thing to appointan in- , spector to pay surprise visits on these sell() -)1s, and in that way be able to see whether the masters were doing their work in a proper manner. (Apptause.) The programme was then proceeded with, a prologue being given by a smart youngster named Percy Lam- bert. The first part of the entertainment consisted of the performance of an operetta " Mr. Nobody." This was given in a most praiseworthy manner, and showed most careful training of the children, reflecting great credit on the teachers. The girls had been trained by Miss Kilburn and Miss Acton; and the boys by the headmaster (Mr. Moultcn) assisted by Mesrs. Kennan, Rosser,and Parr. The following represented the various characters, and the "get up" was all that could be desired—Nobody, Master Samuel Lane; Mischief, Master James Banner; Policeman, Master Wallace McQuinn ; Old Peter, Master William Oliver; Dame Huntley, Miss Beatrice Fleet ; Phyllis, Miss Lily Hill; Dorothy, Miss Evelyn Atherton. The singing of the chori $ ,s and the solos wes excellent, in fact the whole performance was a thorough success. Mr. Clement Handley and Mr.Eigar Lea manipulated the limelight apparatus, and Mr. Ca.l- - provided the scenery, which represented a wood. During an interval the prizes were distributed by Mr. Tomkinson. As evidence of the regular attendance of some of the recipients it may be mentioned that some had attended school, two, three, and even four years without missing a single attendance. Mr. Tornkinson in the: course of a short address, spoke of the pleasure it had given him to witness the entertainment, and com- plimented the head master and teachers eu its success. The following received prizes :

At Runcorn ,Police Court, on Sanirday morning, Mr. J. E. Worsley, coroner, held an inqueot on the body of Ann Leigh, 4S, Budge-st., woo died sud- denly during Thursday night.—James,Leigh,pattern maker, said that his wife had not been in the best .of health for some wEeks, but nithing serious was apprehended. It was .15 months since she was at- tended by Dr. Mangan. She went to bed on Thurs- day night, and on awakening at 4.30 next morning Mr. Leigh found her dead.--Dr.Mangan said he had .knoac n the deceased,some years, and when attt nd- ing her over twelve months ago she was suffering from paralysis. In his opinion the cause.ol death, was due to a further attack, and she died from 'brain disease. A verdict of "Death from natural 'causes" was recorded.

div.head: NEWTON DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: NEWTON DISTRICT COUNCIL.
WARGRAVE WARD.

In support of the candidature of Dr. Mouncey for the Warerave Ward, a meeting was held in the Wargrave Schools on Wednesday evening. Mr. W. Halson pre- sided, and there were with him on the platform. Dr. Mouncey, and Messrs. Cordingley and Williams. 'there was a very fair attendance of electors.—The Chairman said that being the list opportunity they should have of , meeting together, he should like to make a few remarks with regard to a speech made at the Vulcan last week. It was stated that they had a security wit,h their candid- ates, and that Dr. Mouncey's supporters had no security with their candidate. Dr. Mouncey had been before them about 10 years, and had been in and out of the ward by day and night, and was a gentleman who whee he said a thing, meant it. Dr. Mouncey also was acquainted with the water and drainage questions and would be able to bring his knowledge of these matters on the Board. He asked them to support a gentleman whe was his own master, and had not to give an account to any employer of his stewardship.—Dr. Mouncey said he had come before them to refute certain statements, I and also an accusation made against him. In his last I address he advocated the employment of a disinfecting apparatus, and he had heard it said that lie was advoc- ating the spending of too much money. They had got to face the fact that at no distant date they would have to cope with their infectious diseases without outside help, and they must have a more effectual way of dis- infecting clothes, See, or they must have an infectious hospital. The cost of a hospital would be very great, but in the case of a disinfecting apparatus, the cost would be small comparatively, as one suitable for this district could be obtained for about £35 or £4O, and the cost of maintenance would be nothing except when in use, so that, between the two, what he advocated would b 3 the least costly. He was also called to account for advocating a fire engine and brigade. He sod t was an absolute neces- sity that this district should have a fire engine and volunteer brigade for the use of any elector who demanded it. The cost would be comparatively small, as they could get a manual eneine to send a stream nt water in the air 90 feet, for £32. This would be suffi- cient for extinguishine fires in connection with cottage property, but for works they would want a larger engine, and if the works would subscribe towards its cost, as he thought they ought to. do, then they could have a larger one, er even a steam engine. One of the candidates for that ward had spoken in favour of a school Board, but he (Dr. Mouncey) did not think it was neces- sary. Rather let them press for iacreased accommoda- tion in the present voluntary schools, and they could postpone the coming of a School Boord to Earle-Ft-own for some time longer. With regard to the enseEion of diseased meat being sold on the Earlestown market, he was charged with having kept this fact a secret locked within his own breast. That he considered a slander, as it was a notorious fact, and was plentifully ad vertised in daily papers some seven or eight years ago, tha'.; diseased meat was sold on the Earlestown market. He maintained there ought not to be any fool sold,which was not liable to inspection, but in a district like that, which was notorious throughout Lancashire, no inspec- tion whatever was male. How could he a new corner to:the district propose to teach the Commissioners their business or the Medical Officer his duty. What he had been doing, and was still doing, was to warn people against eating meat not sufficiently cooked. He denied directly that he had kept any secret and asserted that such a misrepresentation Or misreading of what he had said, reflected no credit upon Mr. Catterall or those gentlemen who supported him. Next Monday the great fight Came, and he trusted they would do their best to return him as their representative, and he wcialci do all in his power to guard their interests, and endeavour to eive justice to al/. (appliuse.)—Mr. Williams m,ved the following resolution. " Having heard the address of our candidate, Dr. Mouncey, this meeting of rate- payers have every confidence that he will do his best to give entire satisfaction, and we pledge ourselves to do our utmost to secure his return to the Council."—Mr. Cordingley seconded, and the motion was unanimously carried,—A vote of thanks to the Chairman terminated the meeting. TOWN HALL WARD.

In support of the candidature of IMesers. Evans, Rat- cliffe and Gilmour as District Councillors for the Town Hall ward, a meeting was held in the Town Hall, Earles- town, on Tuesday evening. The Rev. E. R. Davies pre- sided, and he was accompanied on the platform by Forrester, Parr, Stringer, Latham, and the can- didates.—The Chairman, after dealing with the benefits and advantages to be derived from the Parish Councils Bill, alluded to want of a public reading room, although Earlestown was placed in ae excellent position as re- garded the Viaductllnstitute and Library. He believed the candidates on the platform were men of sound judgment, and they had had considerable experience in relation to the social government of the town. (Ap- plause.)—Mr. G. Ratcliffe explained that lie was chair- man 44t the Sanitary Committee of the present Board, and he took credit for the committee for the sanitary condition of the district, about which so much had been said. The death rate was 10.8 per 1,000, Red no place in England could favourably with that. The night soil question via,: of very groat importance. and they would have to deal with it in the hest possible manner, to save the ra,.tepayers' pockets. He was willing to go in for reasonable and just improvements, and he did not think any man in the ronm would want them to go in for any- thing unreasnnable. (Hear, hear.) He was also a can- didate as a guardian. no had been on the Board for the last 10 years, and had done his duty fairly to every- one in the township. gear, hear.) He had been three years chairman of the House Committee, two years vice- chairman, and one year as chairmln of the Board of Guardians, and he hoped they would show their trust by electing him on Monday next. (Applause.)— Mr. W. Gilmour at the outset took an opportunity of refuting several statements which had been circulated respecting him, more particularly with regard to an allegation that he had objected to money being voted by the Co-cperative Society for the relief of the oalliers during the e -al strike,and he produced proof from the secretary and chairman of the society, that he had moved the resolution voting £5O towards the relief fund. Ho defied any man to say that he had run away from any public duty that he undertook. There were several questions affecting the township which re• quired attention. Were they protected as they ought to be by the police in this district ? He said, "No," distinctly. They had six policemen, and there was only one doing duty during the day in the whole of Buries. town. The County Council was the body to deal with that question, and he was surprised that the Newton representative had not taken it up. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. E. T. Evans explained at some length his views on the various matters affecting the township, and hoped they would return himself and colleagues by a triumphant majority.—Mr. P. Parr moved, "That this meeting considers Messrs. Evans, Gilmour, and Ratcliffe are fit and nreper persons to represent them in this ward on the District Council, and also that Mr. George Ra.teliffe is a fit and proper person to reprefent the ward on the Board of Guardians, and that we do all we can to fur- ther their interests and secure their election."—Mr. J. Ladiam secondid.and after Mr. Clare and Mr. I). Fnrrefs- ter had spoken in support,it was put to the meeting and carried.

A meetine in connection with the candidature of Mr. M. Winstanley for the Viaduct ward. was held in Sr. John's Mission Hall. Earinstown, on Wednesday evening. 'I he Rev. T. R. Matthews presided and there was a very fair attendance of electors. After a brief introduction by the Chairman. Mr. Win.,tani,..v, made a lengthy address in which he dealt with the duties of the Surveyor. He asserted that the duties of the Surveyor should be divided, and other men appointed, maintaining that by , this moans they would ha v. the work done better. He proceeded to deal with several matters connected with the townQhip, such as the ni.tht soil. sewaee, eas meter rents, street making, drl., and concluded by asking those present to support him on Mnndly.

Divies presided, and there was a largo number of electors present. Addresses were given by each of the candidates on the current questions, and a resolution pledging the meeting. to use every legitimate effort to return the three candidates was adopted.

PROPOSED REDUCTION OF DUES AT LIVERPOOL. The Traffic Committee of tho Liverpool Dock Board have decided to reduce the dock and town dues on cotton is. 4d. a ton, to meet the competition of the Manchester r;hip Canal. This will only apply to cotton " direct override." that is not for storage in Liverpool, but for forwarding to Manchester and else- where. In some quarters this is not approved, as ware- housemen would prefer to have cotton stored, and not sent away from the town, as the now rates will induce. There will probably be cAnsiderable discussion before this Is confirmed by ttie Dock Board as a whole.

At the St. John's Nilsson room 00 Monday even- ing, a lecture was given by Mr. Henry Goldstone, police court missionary of the Diocesan C.E.T.S. on " rescue work at the gate of Walton Gaol, in the Police Court. &c.” The room xv,s filled, chit fly with children, who had evidently flocked there to wit- ness the lime light. views with which the lecture was illustrated. The Rev. T. R. Matthews presided and bri, fly introduced the subject. Recitations were given by Mr. Henry Taylor of Warrington. police court missionary, and songf4 were rendered at intervals by members of St. John's Church choir. The lantern was worked by Mr. W. Lawson, and the lecture which was descriptive of the rescue work carried out under the auspices of the Church of England Temperance Society, was very interest- ing.—A collection was made at the close in aid of the work.

CHILDREN'S ENTERTAINMENT AT HAYDOCIC. On Monday and Tuesday evenings an entertainment was given in the National Schoolroom, Haydock, by the children attending the school. On Monday evening the affair was presided over by Mr. W. S. Barrett, and on Tuesday evening by Mr. T. D. Grimlie Drayton. On each evening there were crowded audiences, who thoroughly enjoyed the various items which were sub- mitted. The programme included choruses, dialogues, duets, comic songs, dances, and nigger sketches. f'svo sketches of an amusing character were also given, en- titled "The District Couneil of Spendingtown," and "Advice gratis." The children had been tutored by Mr. Walden and the teachers, and acquitted themselves in a praiseworthy manner. BAKER'S SOIREE AT EARLESTOWN. The second annual tea party, concert and ball, under the auspices of the Earlestown bakers, took place on Saturday evening in St. John's Hall, Earlestown. There were abont 200 persons preaent to tea, which was of an enjoyable character. A public meeting in connection with the United King- dom Alliance, under the auspices of the Earlestown District Cetnrnittee, was held in the Town Hall, Earles- town, on Friday evening. Being market night there was only a moderate attendance, hut otherwise the meeting was most successful. The Rev. F. E. Miller presided, and he was accompanied on the platform by Councillor Postleth ciaite, of Manchester, Rev. C. F. Aked, Liverpool, and Mr. F. W. Hall, Birkenhead. Powerful addresses were delivered by each of these 2entlemen, on Temperance matters, and a resolutien in support of the local Veto Bill was passed. WARG RAVE CHURCH, EARLESTOWN. A musical service was given in the above church, on Sunday afternoon, by the choir and organist in aid of the choir funds. Triere was a very lazes(' audience, but the collection which was made at the close was only of a meagre character, the amount realised being £3 15s. The various items were submitted in a manner which left nothing to be desired, and were evidently fully ap- preciated by the people present. The following was the programme :—Chorus, "All ,we Hire sheep" ; air, " Why do the nations," Mr. George Wright ; solo and chorus, "Hear my prayer," Miss F. Kean ; organ solo (a) " Allegretto " (Lobgesang Symphony) ; solo, "The Children's Home," Mr. James Nichols ; solo, "The Heavenly King," Miss K. C. Cerlett ; air, "It is enotieh " (Elijah). SHOP ASSISTANTS' BALL AT EARLHSTOWN. The sec-md annual ball held under the auspices of the Earlestown shop assistants, took place in the Town Hall, Earlestown, on Wednesday evening. The hall had bern nicely draped by Mr. E. T. Evans and presented an enlivening appearance. Dancing commenced at nine o'clock, there being upwards of 60 co:iples present. Music was supplied by Mr. Peplow's string band, and the dancing was kept up with much spirit until about 4.30 on Thursday morning. • Mr. J. Millington and Mr. Broderick officiated as M.C.'s, and the catering for the inner man was loelced after by Messrs. Birkhead Bros.

OPENING OF A READING 110051. On Monday evening, the wor;imen's dining-room in connection with the Vulcan Foundry Company's Loco- motive Works was opened as a reading and recreation room for the use of the employes. The interior has under- gone a complete renevation at the expense of the com- pany. There were present at the formal opening Mr. W. Coßingwood, general manager ; Mr. W. Norman, works manager ; Mrs. Norman ; Messrs. James %right :led W. Price, foremen; and about 70 of the employes.— Mr. Collingwood presided, and in opening the proceed- ings said it gave him greatikpleasure to meet the employes on such an interesting occasion, for he felt sure it was a step in the right direction, and he should be pleased to help on the good work. If the workmen tried to help themselves they would be assisted in every way possible. He hoped they would not let the institution die away. Mr. Norman then read a code of rules which had been drawn up. He trusted they would be acceptable. (applause.)—The rules were unanimously agreed to.— Mr. Wright said that now that Mr. Collingwoed and Mr. Norwood had set the stene rolling it was for thern to keep it going, and not let it grow over with moss and fade away as it did when there was a similar effert put forth 48 years ago. On that occasion, the late Edward Tayleur went to considerable expense in providing re- quisites for a library and reading room at the school- room in the village. But it soon died a natural death. He hoped the present employes would apprecia.ta the Privilege which was before them.—Mr. Collingwood then declared the room open.—Mr. and Mrs. Norman then presented to the room two draught boards and men cemplete, two chess hoards and one luilma board com- plete and two sets of dominoes, Mrs. N.irman's niece and Mr. W. Thompson, jun., contributing one en cb of the boards, the remainder being given by Mr. :and Mrs. Norman. Votes of thanks to Mr. Caallingvrood and Mr. Norman terminated the proceedings. The room 'sill be open on week-days only from 6.30 p.m. to ten p.m. The company through Mr. Colliogavorel and Mr. Norman have provided a dressing-room for ;he benefit of the Cricket and Football Out,. MASONIC INSTALLATION AT ASHTON. An interesting gathering of Masons belonging to the Lodge of Faith N0.484,t00k place at the Masonic Reentia, Gerard Arms Hotel. Ashton,on Tuesday, to celebrate the festival of St. John, and to instal Bro. A. Jackson S.W., as the W.M. for the ensuing year. The installing cere- mony was very ably carried carried out by Bro. Har- wood, P.M., I .P.M., and he was assisted by Bro. A. Skeen as D.C. There was a full attendance of brethren, the visitors including Bro. Waring (Leyedty) and Bro. Anderton (S) (Makerfield). After being installed the newly-elected W.M. proceeded to inve6t his officers for the year as follows t—Bros. F. Harwood P.M. 1.P.M.,W. Gilbert S.W.,Thoi.Ritchie J.W ~Rev.E.W. Whittenhury- Kaye Chap. At the close of the inves- titure the brethren sat down to an excellent repast to which ample justice was done. " Installing and Past Masters," Bro. Aspinall, "Officers of the Lodge," Bro. A. Skeen, "All Poor and Distressed Masons," by the Chaplin. THE DISTRICT COUNCIL ELECTION.

The election of district Councillors for Newton district Council will take place on Monday next. The ballot papers for Town Hall, Viaduct and Crow Lane Wards will he counted at the Town Hall, and the results for those wards will be declared there. The pfpers for Wargrave and Newton Wards will be counted in their respective wards, and the results declared in each ward by the deputy returning officers. The following is a list of the presiding officers and poll clerks :—Crow Lane Ward : Polling at Wesleyan Schools, Cross Lane. Mr. G. Burgess,presiding officer. Mr. F. Ball, poll clerk. The poll will open at 12 noon and close at 8 o'clock in the evening. CHILDREN'S ENTERTAINMENT AT NEWTON. At St. Mary's Hall, on Thursday evening, a musical and dramatic entertainment was given by the children of St. Mary's Catholic School, Newton. 'There was a crowded audience and the children who had been trained by the head mistress, Miss Smith and her assistants, went through the programme in an excellent manner. The items included a cantata "The Children's Queen," miseellaneous songs, by St. Mary's "juvenile minstrels," and the comedy" My Aunt's Heiress," the characters being sustainsd by the children. Wharton. A vote Of thanks to the entertainers brought the meting to a el, 'Si'.

OVERCROWDING A 'Bus At the Borough Court on Monday, Frank Naylor, 'bus driver, 61 Wakefield-street, woe charged with having on December 2nd unlawfully crowded a 'bus of which he was driver.—P C. Hollingworth stated that at 820 on the day in question he was at Market Gate when the defendant drove past with fourteen adult passengers. The 'bus was only registered to carry 12 and was on its way to Latchford.—The Mayor said he himself had seen buses overcrowded and he thought it was time the off- ence was put a stop te. Defendant who pleaded not guilty was fined ss. and costs. FURIOUS DRIVING. On Monday. at the Borough Police Court, Thomas Brookes, cattle dealer. Statham, was charted with driv- ing furiously on Knat3ford-road on the 29th November'. Defendant pleaded not guilty.—P.C. Turner deposed to Seeing defendant, about 7.40 on the 29th of last menth, drive a gig at a pace of about 16 miles an hour in Knuts- ford-road. He followed and found the gig standing out- side the "Cheshire Cheese" with no one in charge. He did not sea defendant at the time but later on he again Saw him driving furiously past Belmont Terrace with another man. Both were under the influence of liquor. Corroborative evidence Wag given be two men who were With the officer,and defendant was fined 53. and CO9!:s. Samuel Bell.cab driver,66 Garibahli-sureet,was charged with committing the sema offence in Wilson-Patten- street on the 13th November. He pleaded guilty. P.C. F.Conper proved the case and defendant having a previ- ous good character was let off on payment of is. WIFE DESERTION.—SEVERE PENALTY. At the Borough Police Court. on Saturday morning, Thomas Gilligan WAS charged with running away from the borough of Warrington in Juoe,lB92,leavine, his wife and two children chargeable to the Warrineton Union, Mr B. Shearer, enquiry officer, prosecuted, and Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, defended. Mr. Shearer Bud the pri- soner's wife and two children, aged 6 and 4 years, res. pectivelc. were adteitted to the workhouse on the 13th June. 1892. and since then they had only been out of the workhouse 22 days and had cost the Union £B6. On Friday night the defendant came to Mr. Shearer's office, not knowing that there was a warrant out for hii apprehension, to make inquiries about his family. Be was at once arrested, Mr. Browne, for the defence, con- tended that defendant had left Warrineton on an agree- ment with his wife to get work. During the 2.,e- years he was away he had written three letters home. and had never had any regular work, therefore being unable to send money for the maintenance of his family. Defend- ant had a previous good charac"er.—The magistrates, however, took an extreme view of the caw, and sent him to gaol for three months' hard lahotir. SIX MONTHS FOR FALSE PIRITENCES. On Wednesday at the Borough Police Court, a res. pectably-dressed man, who gave his name as Arthur EVRHS,Wan charged with being on the enclosed premises of Wm. Macaulev, 166, Winwick-road, for unlawful pur- poses on Tuesday, and he was further charged with obtaining food and lodgings by means of a trick. from Ann Craik, 8, Firth-place,on Tuesday night. The Chief Constable said that in the fir t cese the complainant was Elizabeth Macauley. On Tuesday morning defendant met her and styling himself a ticket collector, last from Liverpool,succeeded in obtaining admission to her house as a lodger. Later on in the same merning P.C.B Arnett met with a gentleman near the Horse and Jockey, Winwick-road, who after saying his name was rravis, from Edgehill. told the constable that he had just seen a man who he knew, had run away from his ledeinge at. Edgehill, Liverpool, without paving, and taking some articles with him. A deectiptinn was given of the man and the gentleman accompanied Barnett to Mrs. Macau- ley's and found defendant there. When brought down to the Police Station sevenl articles were found upon defendant, but nothing nf an incriminating, nature. In the second case. Mrs. Craik w 55 the comolainant. It appears that defendant wee questioned at the Police station as to where he had slept the previous night, and aster making several false statements told the police that he had been at Firth-niece. Inspector Spirits there- upon visited Mr. Craik and elicited that defendant had gone through the same rigmerole, and made effete: fer board. Mr. Hunt said he had reason to believe that defendant was wanted for similar off 4res at Liverpool and Widnes. Defendint admitted this and made no de- fence.—He ve,s sent to gaol for three months' herd labour on each cherge (six months in ell).

thus eight points ahead. Tyldegley failed to furthe increase their lead, although they made Ntrenuous efforts to do so. The Warrington defence was too safe. Heesocn, Boscow, and Buxton being especially so. When the whistle blew for the cessation of hostilities, Warrington had sustained their first defeat at home this season, by a

goal and a try to nil. WARRINGTON* V. TYLDESLEY "A " TEAMS.— rile War- rington "A" team journeyed to Tyldesley on Saturday, and were defeated. They were rather unfortunate throughout the gam., having hard lines in not scoring early on, and for the rest of the play they had either twe or three enen off, one player hurting his shoulder, another getting a kick which temporarily disabled him, and a third meeting with some other slight mishap. Had Fyldesley not won under such circumstances they vesuld have been poor players indeed. As it was, how- ever, the game was by no means of a runaway charac- ter. Tylcksley were continually exhorted by the spec- titters to play with their feet, and when they did play with their feet they certainly had a slight advantage. But when it came to playing with the headn.when it was the science that told, Warrington had be far the best of the play. In the passing department, Warrington were far and away ahead of their oppsuents, and the Tykles- , ley spectators vrere greatly surprised to find what a solenoid passing game the Warringtonians played. Tyldesley endeavoured at times to imitate them, but ' they lost ground on each occasion, and were met with loud cries of "Play svi' yer feet," and accerdingly they resumed the style of play for which they are apparently distinguished. The journey to Teldesley was made via Manchester, the train service through Kenyon on the L. and N.W. railway being se inconvenient and slow. Tylclesley was reached in good time, but the teams were twenty minutes late in appearing nn the field. The referee appointed failed to fulfil his engagement, and a spectator took his place and gave satisfaction, except as to his decision regarding the first try. Warrington kicked off, and preventing a return commenced to press their opponents, and twice were within an Ice of getting over. However, Tsidesley relieved, and throughout the rest of tie first half the play was of a give and take character, neither side being able to score. In the second half, Tyldesley succeeded in getting two tries Warrington having two men off at the time. As regards the first try, it is doubtful whether the ball should not have been ruled hack, on the ground that it had been knocked on. The Warrington players expected that the ball would be called hack, and did not make any serious attempt to prevent the homesters getting over. Tne latter, however, followed the hall up and placed it ow the line, the referee allowing the try. The visitors a"r peered clisheartentd after this, and very shortly afteP- wards Tylclesley scored a second try. Ormernd scorer; the first and Miller the second. The place kicks failed° the hall in each case striking the upright. The gam, ended in a victory for Tvldesley by two tries to nil, Teams ~..—Warrington Mannion, full back : Moores. Lewless. div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.

Runar Fogra ALL. There was one section of spectators upon the War- rington ground on Saturday, who were jubliant, but it was not the home lot. The Tyldesley team had brought a large number of supporters with them, and this portion could frequently be heard on Saturday after- noon. Notwithstanding the good record Tyidssley have had this season, the Warrington team fully expected to hold their own with them, for they did not forget that last year, Tyldesley were doing almost equally as well as this season, but had to put up with a•defeat of a goal and a try to nil. The boot was on the other leg on Ssturday, however, much to the chagrin of Warrington, and strange to say, the score was a goal and a try again.

Tyldeslev have done remarkabls; well this year, only havipg suffered one defeat in the league cenapetition,aad that was at the hands of S. Helens. This one defeat of ceurse is not surprising, for Tyldesl9y appear to be utter- ly unable to defeat Sr. Helens. Tyldesley have just as good a record as Oldham, and Oldham will have to look out for Nualls when they meet the " Bongers."

I was glad to notice that Barber had again donned the Warrington jersey. and that he had thrown his lot in with the Warrington team. He was very early prominent in the match and his rare turn of speed. and fearless tackling made him very prominent all through the match.

The department in which Warrington lo.vt the game was the forward. The Tyldesley forward are an excepl-ion• ally strong lot, and were much superior to the Warring- ton eight. This was especially noticeable during the concluding portion e, f the ga.me,when the Tyldegley men did pretty much as they chose. Din made his first appearance before a Warrington crowd since he was chosen to represent Lancashire and he was received with a loud outburst of applause. He kept up his form, and was the most hard-working forward on the field.

In the half back division, Bate and Clarke were op- posed to the brothers Berry, and they had a lot to con- tend with. " Buff " Berry has not lost any of his wiles, and he is still a most dangerous player. Warrington now possess a capital lot of threequarters, and if they could get the ball often enough, they would bother the other side a lot. The olk fault of keeping the hall to the forwards and halves, however, was still in evidence on Saturday. It was very rarely that the ball was passed out of the scrimmage to the threequarters, and as a cOnsequence, Burton, Cunningham, Heesom, and Barber had to make all their play. This is not as it should be, and the players ought to practice pas4ing more than they do at present. The two wings, Barber and Burton were scarcely given a fair chance to distinguish them- selves. Barber ought certainly to have been fed more than he was.

But if the threequarters were not given much chance to attack,they with Boscow defended capitally. Boscow as usual, was quite safe, and was the means of repelling numerous assaults of Tyldesley. He is without doubt, one of the best full backs in the county. The result of the match is not very far wrong. In the first half the teams were very equal, and the game for the greater part raged at half way. But in the second half the Tyldesley team wore down on their opponents, and held the upper hand almost all the time. The second try, fenm which the goal was kicked, was not a vvry satis- factory one. The try was awarded on the ground that Evans was obstructed. However, Warrington were beaten befm.e then,and only their average can be spoiled by the circumstance.
The league tab'e has been altered this week, and War- rington droni from third to fourth place, St. Helens go- ing up on the list. The following is the result. up to date :

To-day, Warrington journeys to Manchester to meet the once powerful Manchester team. Last year, the Mancurians rather unexpectedly heat Warrington by a try to nil, hut Warrington on that occasion made the journey, via. the Manchester Ship Canal, and the sail apparentlY did not agree with them. To-day, they go by the old-fashioned railway, and therefore they will tint get any of the 'zone from the district round Barton. 'The followinc, is the team selected to represent War- ringtnn :—full hack, Boscow ; three-quarters, Barker, Moores, Heesom, ard Burton ; halfbacks. Bare and Nevins : forwards, Turner, Jolley, Dskin, Berry,Taylor, Buckley, Bailey, and Andrews. The A team lost at Tyldesley on Saturday, and thus were able to sympathise with their seniors. They were however more unlucky than the first team, for they had the hest of the game all through. Casualties to players caused their defeat, for no fewer than three players were hurt during the match. At the time the two tries were obtained by Tyldesley, Warrington were two men short. Under these circumstances, it is not sutprising that the team was defeated. The first try obtained by Tyldesley was not a very good one, for there was a suspicion of there having been a knock on. It is not often that a team has so many misfortunes in one match.

--- St. Mary's further increased their average by beating I,Vilmslow byl6 points to nif, and Stockton Beath also beat Runcorn Heereation by a goal and a try t) a try, so that the juniors in this district are keeping it up.

By tbc way what has become of the Rangers ? I can- not get to know how they are gettins., on. I hear now and again about tho second team, but nothing of the first. I hope they are not doing so badly that they are afraid of the public knowing. They havc done some 17,00 d things in the past, and I hope that-they are con- tinuing' to do so now. I only wish to know whether it is so or not.

CYCLING. "Wheeling." one of the leading cycling papers, thus refers to the Wodd's patent saddle manufactured at the Longford works, Warrington :—" T'‘e National Show brought before us a new saddle, which, if we are not much mistaken, will find a large meed of popularity with those who ride for pleasure. It is on the principle involved in the wire woven • mattress of commerce, the top being of fine spirals interwoven, supported at the hack by a semi-circular stay, and brought down in front on either side of the peak piece. Across the centre and underneath is set a fairly strong spring-spiral which gives a great amount of fife to the saddle. The short trial we had of it inclines us to rank it as one of the most comfortable seats we have ever had on a cycle.

THE M AYORESS. In the " Gentlewoman "of last. week appears an excellent portrait of Mrs. James Fairclough amongst a group of "New Mavoreses " • SUCCESSFUL WARRINGTON PUPILS. The following pupils of the Misses Rimier, Wilson Patten-steet, have successfully passed the last practical examination in violin playing : Senior pass, Miss Margaret A. Leigh, Warrington Junior pass, Miss Lily M. Jones, Latchford. Dr• Latt, Principal of the College, was the examiner. .WAItnINGTON RAGGED SCHOOL. The first of a series of lime-light entertainments,
in connection with the above institution, was given in the schoolroom on Saturday evening, the subject

being "Jarnes Conquest," followed by other views. Mr. Lewis George contributed the lantern and views, and was assisted by Mr. Thomas Jones, and Mr. H. Osborne gave the reading. At the close, Mr. Woods contributed a solo. Mr. Woodhouse acted as

accompanist. There was a good attendance CONCERT AT ST. PAUL'S INFANT SCHOOL. The series of entertainments which were com- menced a short time ago in St. Paul's Infant school- room, .Kendrick-st., were continued on Saturday evening. The Rev. E. 11. Townsend occupied the chair, and there wls a very fair audience. An ex- cellent programme was provided, and included a pianoforte duet, by the Rev. 11. V. and Mrs. Pigot, piano and violin duet Miss Chantry. and Miss Leigh, songs by Miss Oxley and Mr. Amos, accompanied by Miss A. Smethurst. The Rev. 11. V. Pigot also gave a reading, "The Olden Times." At the close a hearty vote of thanks was accorded the chairman and artistes. LECTURE ON FERMENTATION._

_ On Saturday night the first of two lectures on fermentation industries, with special reference to bread making, was given in the lecture room at the Museum by Mr. James Grant, of the Manchester Technical School. The lecturer, after dealing with the theories of some of the early scientists, went on to show how moulds, yeasts, and bacteria were mused. The lecturer, who concluded amid applause, remarked that the lecture that night was more an introduction to the lecture to be given next Satur- day than anything else. At the close of the lecture those who wished, were allowed to look through the microscope at some samples of moulds and

yeasts. CONCERT AT SMITH-STREET SCHOOL. On Monday evening, a concert was given by the ' girls of the Smith-street School, in the Bank-street Mission, when there was a large attendance. The concert consisted of the Juvenile Cantata " Play- plater; " which was rendered by the girls in a manner which earned for them well-merited applause. The following were the characters :—Mother Goo;e,Miss Parkinson; Jack Goose, Jane Lawless; Farmer Jack,Mary Daniels; Cowboy Jack,Sa.rah 1-It)ughtoa ; Dick Wittington, Elizabeth Webb; Annie Laurie, Isabel Massey ; Maggie Lauder, Annie Miller; Flora Macdonald, Dora Taylor; Simple Simon, Lottie Glieve; and Aunt Sally, Sarah Wright. - These were assisted. by a strong chorus, and a pleasant evening was brought to a close about 9.30 by the singing of
the National Anthem. SALE OF WOES IN WYCLIFFE HALL.

A sale of work in aid of the Church Funds and Home and Foreign Missions was held in the Wycliffe Hall, Bewsey-street, on Wednesday after- noon. Only a portion of the Hall was made use of, being divided from the remainder b 3 curtains hung with flags and draperies. There were two large and attractive looking stalls containing fancy goods, underclothing, woollen materials, and other tastefully made articles for ornamental and other uses. A large and inviting refreshment stall was also provided where eatables of all descriptions could be procured. The goods hare been made and given by members of the : congregation and friends--Mrs. Z. Armi- tage, Mrs. Barker, Mrs. W. Wallington, Mrs. P. T. Winskill, Mrs. J. W. Jeffery, Miss Garner, Mrs. Porritt, Ntiss Pickarance, Mrs. Wylie, and Mrs. J. Yonge, for the management of the fancy goods' stalls and the business of the refreshment stall was conducted by Mrs. Garland, Mrs. Walker, Mrs. J. Birtles, the Misses Birtles and Miss Harrison. The net amount realised was £36. WILL OF THE LATE MR. CHARLES LISTER. Probate has been granted in respect ot the w;.

of the late Mr. Charles Lister, of Awien Hall,Lvmm, Cheshire, the amount of the estate being sworn at £70,561 te. 71., which includes freeholds. Mrs Alice Lister, the widow,is appointed sole executrix and trustee, and the deceased bequeathed to her his house, household furniture, horses, carriages, &c., and a legacy of £5OO. To his mother the sum of £lOO is bequeathed ; to his mother-in-law £5O; to each of his friends, Mr. John Archibald Russell, Q.C., and the Rev. T. F. Clarke, Vicar of Rostherrie as a slight memento, the sum of 19 guineas; and to his sons on attaining the age of 25 years the sum of £5,000, such legacies to carry interest. To his wife he bequeathed if, and when she marries again, the sum of £5,000 absolutely; to the Vicar and church- wardens of Rostherne the sum of £2OO upon trust to be invested far the repair and maintenance of the four stained glass windows erected by himself,Mrs. Listerond their children in the Parish church ; and also £lOO to the Vicar and churchwardens to be paid to the sexton for keeping his grace in good order. As regards the remainder of his estate it is divided amongst the members of his family. WARRINGTON CONSERVATIVE CLUB, ANNUAL MEETING. - - -

The annual meeting of the members of the above club was held on Monday evening,, under the pre- sidency of Alderman Francomb, J.P. Mr. Pilling read the annual report, which stated that the club during the past twelve months had been well at- tended, and conducted in a most satisfactory manner. In May last there was a change in the managership, Mr. Higham having decided to leave Warrington to commence business for hinn-,;elf in Southport. The committee appointed Mr. George Watkins, of Attercliffe, Sheffield, to fill the vacancy. The committee deplored the loss through death of some of their best members during the year, namely their good and kind friends Sir Gilbert Greene'', Alderm an Ashton, Mr. Lewis Voisey, Mr. Charles Skinner, Mr. J. V. Taylor, Sze. Councillor Srae,th- burst moved, and Councillor Dr. Caunell seeondter the adoption of the report, which was agreed to. In the absence of the treasurer (Mr. William Owen), Alderman Wright presented the financial statement which was passed. Mr. Pilling was re-elected secre- tary, Mr. Owen treasurer, and the committee were re-elected. Votes of thanks were accorded to these gentlemen, as well as to Mr. Robert Pierpoint. for his gift of a valuable dictionary to the library. Alderman Francomb was thanked for his services in the cnair, and the meeting terminated. CONCERT AT BOLD-ST, WESLEYAN SCROOL. gram] concert under the auspices of the Young People's Society of Christian Endeavour, was held in the Bold-st. schoolroom, on Monday evening. The Rev. Cr. D. Mason presided, and there was a good attendance. The band under the conductor- ship of Mr. Pendlebury, which does duty every Sunday afternoon at the "Services for the People " in Bold-st. Wesleyan Chapel, was present at the concert., and opened the programme by a gavotte, Theodore" (Ch. le Thiere), which was performed in a masterly manner. Later in the evening they played the selection, " Rosarounde" (Schubert),and the intermezzo, "Sunset" (A. E. Matt), for the latte r of which they were deservedly encored. Miss ' Steel and Miss Brown's voices blended together very beautifully, and they were heard to advantage in "When the wind bloweth in 7 (S mart), and "In the dusk of the twilight" (Parker), for the latter of which they were obliged to respond to an en- core. "Out on the Deep" (F. C. [Joke), and "Be- (bum's love Song," were well interpreted by Mr. :Rudolph Hiller. Miss Florence G. Hiller was the favourite of the eveninpind she sang with exceed- ingly good taste, " We will wander" (Victor Mon- crief), and " For all eternity" (Angelo Moseheconi), for the latter of which the audience would not be refused an encore, and to which she responded by singing the popular song, "Daddy." A number of elections were also played on the instruments. A pianforte solo was well rendered by Mr. J. W Cheedle, entitled, "Novellette" (Schumann). and Miss j. E. Pigot and Mrs. G. D. Maeon ably played as a pianoforte duet, "Polnieche Tanze " X. Schar- wenka). • Mr. Adcrolt upon the clarionet, and Mr. Podmore upon the flute received loud applause for their interpretation of, "Lo hear the gentle lark" (Bishop), and " Morceau" (C. G. Reissiger), were, charmingly rendered as a trio by Mr. W. Brown, violin ; Mr. E. Balmford, 'cello,and Miss J. E.Pigot. piano. Miss J. E. Pigot and Mr. J. W. Cheedle per- formed the duties of accompanists. An excellent programme was brought to a termination by the band playing the march, "Grand Festal" (C. Wright).

div.head: INSPECTION OF CANAL BOATS
div.p: THE INSPECTION OF CANAL BOATS

Mr. Brydon, chief inspector under the Canal Boats Acts, wrote a letter, drawing the attention of the auth- ority t the neglect of Inspector Farrington to carry out the duties entrusted to him in connection with the Canal Boats Act. It the Inspector had not time to devote to this work, the Authority should make such an arrang,.- ment as would ensure the fulfilment of the duty which had been imposed upon the Authority by Statute. Inspector Farrington had written to Mr. Brydon in respect to tile matter and pointed out that he had only been able to make two inspections, comprising eleven boats. During the past year his work had been some- thing fearful and he felt that he could not hold out much longer at the same rate of movement. He had not had a single Sunday clear for the past twelve months and he had not slept out of his district for the past seven years.—Mr. Aaron said their Inspector had entirely too much work to do, hnd he could rot be expected to perform it all.—lnspector Farrington further explained that there was no terminus in his district—the boats were always on the move. There was a marked . improvement in the condition of canal boats. There had only been one prosecution necessary in three years.—Mr. Woodward pointed out that the members did not consider that Mr.*Farrifigton had been remiss in his duties. There was no doubt that there had been a great deal of infectious disease pre- vailing in the district throughout the year.—Mr. Hey- wo-,cl proposed that a reply be sent by Mr. Ashton to the effect that they had triken the matter up with Mr. Farrington, who had promised to pay better attention to the inspection in future. They were aware he had numerous nuisances to inspect,and these had prevented him from fulfilling the duties. The resolution was car- ried.

THE SMALLPDX HOSPITAL AT HOWIE. Mr. Brandretti gave a verbal report of the committee appointed to wait upon the Manchester Ship Canal Co., with reference to the detention of the hospital at Moore ; and as a result of their .consultation Mr. Dunlop pro- mised to reconsider the question of the rent to he paid by the Authority. A vote of thanks was passed to the deputation.

div.head: SAD FATALITY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: SAD FATALITY AT RUNCORN.
THE INQUEST.

Thomas Weston, 18 years of age, apprentice at the Sprinch Works of Manchester Ship Canal Company. at Runcorn, died at his parents' house, 38 Union-street, on Friday, trout injuries he received whilst following his employment. An inquiry into the circumstances was held by Mr. J. E. Woreiey, coroner,at the Runcorn Police Court on Saturday morning. Mr. F. Wiswall, repre- sented the Bridgewater Undertaking of the Manchester Ship Canal Company ; Mr. T. Bewyer was present on behalf of the relatives. The first witness called was the father of the deceased Mr. T. Weston, boiler maker. He said he worked with deceased in the same shop on the previous day, but was not engaged there at the time of the accident. He saw the beam which was being riveted. It was placed on its base, on two good blocks, and was held in position by wooden stays. It was for the men who were work- ing to remove the stays as they proceeded with the job 'They did not trust boys to do work like that. His son was brought home at 9.30 on Friday. Dr. Robinson attended bin:, and found his right leg broken in two places his lett e rat broken, and that he was suffering from internal injuries. Witness saw the beam after the accident, and he thought the cause of its falling must have been the taking away ot some of the props. In his opinion it, was not sufficiently propped. He could not give an exact opinion. There were two sets of men engaged en the work, and no previous mishap had happened. The beam would weigh about two tons.— James Lloyd, overlooker of boiler makers, said he wa present at the time of the accident. He and decease r were going alongside the girder to work at the othe end. He saw it move,, and call «1 to Weston. There were two men on the other side. Witness jumped away and escaped, but the youth put up his arms as though tee hag to guard it from him, arid was caught between it and the boiler. •He was a , -rue ucam was on two blocks, and held in position by wooden shores. It was the duty of the riveters to move the props as they proceeded. Be could not explain why the girder fell over. He considered it was properly fixed. The custom was to have throe shores on each side. Tbe beam was 34 feet long. 'They had not commenced work upon it, but were taking their tools to it. Mr. Weston, the previous witness, was it last. Witness was not aware that it was afterwards touched. He did not think there was a misgiving of any of the props. He could not account for its moving.—By a Juror : He did not know of any larking going on during the bnakfast hour. The machinery had just started.—By another Juror: He could not say that the vibrations of the mechinery would affect it. He could not stateethat any °dire apprentices had played about it, and knocked sure of the stays down. They were not allowed to play in the works. The girder fell over before they touched Wiswall said the falling over of the girder was a mystery to him.—John (Mean of 42, Sewell-street, boiler meker, said he was present at the time of the accident. They had not commenced work upon the opposite side, where nothing was disturbed. Deceased's father placed the prop within two feet of the place where his son was injured.—By Mr. Bowyer :—'They never disturbed the girder.—Samuel Blundell, 30,Albert- street, stated that on the morning of the accident he placed a convex bar at the tap of the girder. There were three wooden props on the side where the accident happened. He did no interfere with the props. There were men in the shop during the breakfast half-hour.— Mr. Wiswall stated that he saw the beam on Thursday. The evidence given re specting the shoring-up was correct so far as he knew. It was the duty of the fitters to remove the props as they advanced ins their Werk. Those employed, for their own sake, had to see there was a proper footing for the shores. Wooden stays Were the safest. If any mischief was done,it was during the breakfast halt hour. It was impossible to gain any mire information if the inquest was adjourned.— Mr. Bowyer said that so far as the engineer was con- cerned he was certain everything was done for the 8 ifety of those engaged.—Mr. Wiswell said they prided themselves in doing all they could to prevent accident, and had the most comfortable workshops in the country. Teev were sorry the accident had happened.—P.C. Reeler-demi atated that he had made inquiries from all in the shop, and they said no one was near the girder during the breakfast half-hour.—The Coroner, in sum- Ming up. said that the only inference was that during breakfast time someone must have interfered with the beam—most probable accidentally. Some cause must have transpired to make it insecure. At all events when the men were preparing to commence work, it fell over. Whether this was because the props slipped, or they accidentally or otherwise removed, was a mystery they had not cleared up. The evidence had been given in a straight-forward manner.—The jury returned a verdict to the effect that deceased died from injuries received by the falling of the girder. They did not think there was sufficient evideece to record a verdict of accidental death.
