WARGRAYE WARD MEETING, EARLESTOWN. DISCLA.I HER. Sir,—At the meeting held at the Vulcan school on the 3rd inst. in support of the candidature of Messrs. Col- lingwood, Slee and Thompson, statements were made which are inaccurate and misleading to the public,and which call for correction. Mr. Collingwood, after re- ferring to a report that he had discharged a workman for smoking when at work, goes on to say that" he was disgusted at people descending to personalities of that sort to further themselves, and did not think that they (the audience) would support men who would descend to things of that sort," thus interring that other candi- dates had circulated this report. Mr. Collingwood has been wrongly informed. We, as two of the candidates, give a most emphatic denial to the above statement. We challenge Mr. Collingweod to prove one instance where this has been done. It was impossible for us to have used this workman's discharge against Mr. Collingwood, for we were not oven aware that a man had been dis- charged, until our a:tention was directed to it after,and in consequence of his speech. The nearest approach to any personality OR .mr part was where public attention was rightly directed to the fact that Mr.Collingwood had only attended 25 out of 84 Board and committee meetings. On the contrary we have studiously avoided personali- ties, and at our meetings have endeavoured to speak pot of persons,but of the subjects likely to be brought before the Council. We do not avow ourselves to be personal opponents of anyone, but simply seek to represent on the Council the direct interests of the workmen and small householders, believing that the Parish Council Act in- tends that every class—not one class—should be so re- presented. We commenced this contest deermined to do or say nothing of which we need be ashamed, and we intend to finish in the same spirit whether we win or lose.—Yours Stc.,

div.head: W. DAVIES. E. C. PRYOR
div.p: W. DAVIES. E. C. PRYOR

sufficient to prevent a man making a display of himself by denying the existence of the embryo in wheat grains. Ben Chayill was a little further advanced in know- ledge of botany than the infelicitous Summers. But where is "Ben Chayell" uow that this ceiestion has ceased to be a matter of opinion werely,and become one of fact and easy experitnentil verification? Can it be that it is not so much the truth these good folk are anxious about, as a cheap victory for their own pre- conceived wrinions ? I promised " Ben " if he would ask for it, an explanation. Although he has not had the grace to do this, nor to apologise for the bad lan- guage he used, I will, by way of heaping coals of fire upon his head, do my best to let in a little light on the actualities of the matter. If " Ben Chayill " will take,a grain of wheat and place it lobed side down, on a table, and with a sharp penknife cut the skin all round the little pit or depression, he will see at one end of the rounded back of the seed and then lift out the little yellow germ, he will observe beneath, its wrinkled integument ; if new, he will place this interesting little stranger on a damp cloth, he will find it to start on the business of life, and, if properly attended to, grcw to maturity. Meanwhile he can keep the rest of the seed unchanged for the remainder of his natural life in order to convince himself that, although the germ has" quickened "there is not even " the verisimilitude to the laws of decay and death of the investiture, the external wrappings and in- teguri,ents of the corn seed." The result of such an ex- _ p-rimant ought to convince the most contentious mind rhat here the dead remain dead, and the living grow into further life without the "great bulk of the corn- seed" furnishing it with any substenance ; the feeding being by common table sugar and other non-living sub- stances, artificially supplied. Where then is " Ben Cheyill " and his Sunday school authority ? who says, "the vast bulk" must all be changed and dissolved—in other words die—in order that the living germ may be nourished and be as fruit." This is fiction ; facts say

no. To use a favourite phrase of our " Ben's" it is the merest " word-mongering" to say that when the living germ feeds upon the non-living nutriment stored for its use, this non-living matter dies. And now a word as to the methods of these commentators. They believe in assertion and re-assertion as argument. They prefer to it down and draw upon their " inner consciousness.," for what they are pleased to call facts. Thus :—Dr. Adam Clarke imagines the bulk of the grain to become a "fine earth " ! While Mr. Felix Summers—in hip infelix opens summa—belies nature to uphold a book, finding it so much easkr to rant about the last rather that to investigate the former. It is certainly amusing to see how these facts are received by different minds. When I brought these facts before the Field Club—representing,l suppose, the cream of scientific Warrington—they were received by absolute undenial—not a word was said against the faets produced. Even the President, having nothing to say, said it in a dissertation on the necessity of faith, and the futility of seeking accurate knowledge !—an attitude at least remarkable in the President of a scienti- fic association; as it seems to cut at the root of his posi- tion and the Society over which he presides. But it is rapidly ceasing to be a damnable heresy to held that "they didn't know everything down in Judee" ! Taking as my warrant for this investigation the test—" Prove all things; hold fast that which is rood," which neces- sarily involves the rejection of what can be proved to be not good, I am constrained to regret as a fallacy the assertion, whether it be found in the Primer of a humbugging botanist or in the" bundle of Hebrew old cloths "—that " the seed must die ere it can quicken." Magna eat veritas, et praTniebit. That is true. Truth is great—but lying tradition is very persistent.— Yours, &c.,

JOHN PEERS. THE IRON TRADE AND FOREIGN COMPETITION. Dear sir,—Will you allow me in the first place to question the correctness of Mr. Moeks' statement with regard to the Welsh Iron Trade. I have every reason to believe that it is still in existence, and the quotations for Welsh iron still appear in the trade newspapers. If it is not in existence, I think it behoves Mr. Monks to state why the country possessing iron in such large quantities of a similar nature and paying lower rates of wages than Belgium has gone out of existence. In the second place I think that Mr. Monks should explain how coal can he delivered at the Belgian works at the same price as in this country when the cost of production is at least 2s. per ton higher in Belgium. Something must be radically wrong in this country if the coal-owners who can pro- duce coal so much cheaper are putting into their pockets more profit than the Belgium coal-owners. With regard to the Belgium ironworkers and Mr. Monks' opinion, I can only say it is not my opinion, but it is the opinion expressed by practical employers who have visited Belgium, and also of one of the Se.lretariee of the Iron and Steel Institute, who, some years ago, visited the whole of the Continental manufacturing dis- trict and made a report with regard to the number of men, and the cost of production; and if it is true as other employers state that three men are required in Belgium to do the work of two in this country, the wages of these rray be 33+ per cent, less, but coat of production the same in both countries. The statement of Mr. Monks that tine total amount paid in Belgium is 63. per ton less than in NVarrineton requires further explanation, and he should at least give the firm he is comparing with, or his figures carry no weiehtand it may he necessary for a deputation of work- men to go to Belgium to prove the fallacy of Mr. Monks' comparisons. Dees Mr. Monks desire to compare best iron works in this country with common iron works in Belgium,"? To have a fair comparison we must have similar qualities of iron and similar processes. Mr. Monks will admit that there is certainly more than 7s per ten difference in the production of best iron as compared with the c)mtnonest of iron. I should also like to call his etention to the fact that the question is of national importance and must be dealt with in a much broader spirit than confining it to Warrington alone; and to see what effect the tr,de has upon War- rington in the figures given by Mr. Monks he should have g • n the exact quantities manufactured in War.' rington. In may be news to Mr. Monks to know that a _gentle. man in the Midlands, Mr. Sparrow, more than 40 efe,rs ego—l believe before the works were established in Wir- rington—used to write foretelling the death of the British iron trade owing to the Belgian competition. It is only just upon occasions when trade is depressed that this cry of foreign competition is used. The statement with regard to machinery and plant is not my statement, but is the statement of a practical eneineer who was mi. in Belgium during the last meet- ing of the Iron and Steel Inst,tute and who made a thorough examination and comparison. Ido not hold myself responsible for these contradictions amongst the employer classes. It may perhaps be as well if Mr. Monks would deal with the home industries and point out to us the causes of the various differences of prices in the United Kingdem. We iind that in the North of England prices are from £1 17s. 61. to £5 2s. ,in Scotland from £5 55. to £5 12s. V., Wales £5 to £5 2s. 6d ,South Staffordshire £5 1,55.i.0 £6 103.. North Staffordshire £5 103. to £7, Lancashire £5 7s. 6.1. If there is not more than 7s. per ton difference in the cost of production between Warrington and Beleium why is there such a variety of prices in these various districts at home, all of these quotations being under the same conditions ?—Yours respectfully,
T. INIALKIN.

div.p: Wargrave-road, Dec. 3rd, 1894. PUBLICANS AND THE ELECTIONS AT EARLP,-;TOWN.

Sr,—From a bill which I have received, I gather that our popular young curate in the Town Ball Ward has severed his connection with one of the gentlemen whose name appears on the joint address. lam very glad of this, for along with many others, I was both surprised and grieved to find two such callings so closely asso- ciated. The tendencies of the public-house to my mind are not religionward. I consider Mr. litye's chances of success will now be improved. lam not in favour of a publican being placed on the Council, nor yet being made a Guardian, neither did I like to vote for any candidate who was running along with such an one. I am pleased the objection i 3 removed. I cannot see how it will be to our interest to elect sellers of alcholic liquor to either Council or Guardians, but I do see seve- ral reasons why they should not be elected. One of the liquor journals says —"It: is most desirable for publi- cans, brewers, &es to secure seats on the new Councils, for erelong the granting of licenses will be entrusted to them." They (the drink-sellers) are urged to capture the new Councils and to use every moans in their power to get elected Guardians. Preparation for the fight has been made months ago. Where are our teetotal friends? The leaders have said, ".t whatever cost of money or labour the organisation of the trade must be strengthened and perfected at every point." " Every place—public- house, merchant's, and grocer's shop at which alcoholic beverages are sold must be made a centre of political activity," and thus "by making their houses centres for political teaching they would soon make any Govern- ment feel their power." This activity has commenced. Lord Roam-bevy says. " That owing to the enormous in- lanence wielded by those interested in the traffic we are approaching perilously near the corruption of our poli- tical system." The close connection between the poor rates and the public-house is. co well kaown and so universally recognised that there is scarcely any need to elaborate the argument or to quote the pr )ofs which mieht be given in the greatest profusion. Every thoughtful ratepayer will perceive that the rule Of drink-sellers would mean high rates and heavy taxes. Judge Fitzgerald says "the results of drink are pauper- ism, destitution, gaols, lunatic. asylums, evorkhou.ee,end the grave." Nineteen twentieths of the crime of the calender is prodnced by drunkennese, " the heaviest tax we have to pay is that produced by intoxication." Gaol chaplains tell us that almost all the crime originates in the public-house ; superintendents of lunatic asylums say the principle cause of madness is drink, and guardians tell U 3 that 80 per cent. of the pauperism both in the workhouse and outside is the product of drink. lam told that three parts of the meney we are compelled to pay for police and poor rates (that is 15-3. out of every pound) is the -direct or indirect resnit of the liquor traffic. Sir, shalt we send brewers, publicans, drinksellers, or nominees of these people to represent Us, presumably to keep down rates, &c., and to relieve the poor, many of whom are there as a direct result of drink, and the liquor dealers are enriched thereby. Shall we send them after this to relieve them (the poor) with ratepayers' •money ? I for one say " No," and on Monday next shall emphasise the same at the polling booth, and trust many others will follow 5t.—Thanking you, Mr. Editor, for allowing space,—l am yours truly, E. LECTOR. Town flail Ward, Earlestown, Dec. 1211, 1894.

to give a better attendance, but the majority would be a great deal worse. He was in favour of the public being admitted to the Council meetings but he thought they would find the debates very dull as the business of the Board was done in committee. He was in favour of " houge to house" visitation as suggested in the Liberal proilainme, and he believed that in the east part of the town that visitation had taken place. But it was found to be perfectly useless to put in any different style of sewage until proper sewers had been provided. There had also been the substitution of water carriage for the , old system, but at present the owner, when he had carried out this improvement had to pay for water. He looked upon that as an oppressive tax and thouF.,,ht that the Authority should give the water free. He also I thought that water should be supplied free to private baths, as the rateable value of a house with a bath was more than one without. During the year they had adopted a new code of byelaws, and lie gave Mr. Wynne linmphries credit for the action he took in that matter. He considered they were a great advantage, especially tinge relating to the building of houses. Referring to the health of the town, he said, that it had so greatly improved that the gravediggers and doctors had almost found their occupation gone. (Laughter.) He agreed most cordially with the Liberal council programme in that part relating to the making of streets and hack piseaees when houses had been built. He thought it was as much the duty of the builder to make the street as to put the roof on the house. (Applause.) Back passaees had been a fearful source of disease, and there were a eond number in a bad condition in Runcorn. Although in faYour ot the provision of baths, h. thought the rates were too high at present to provide them. He was quite in favour of the inspection of canal boats , without respect of persons. Dealing with the question of a graving dock he spoke of the good work done on the Board in this direction by Mr. Ilisbrown. Aceording to the graving dock agreement with the Skip Canal Company, the dock would be placed on the wrong side of Runcorn Bridge—that was to the Warrington side. Large ships would not be able to get under the bridge without cutting their masts, therefore it would he better to have it on the other side of the bridge. The speaker also alluded to a circular he had received from the dock labourers in which they stated that better prevision was required for unloading vessels, and pointed out the large number of vessels which had to he unloaded elsewhere between Eastharn and Runcorn owing to lack of accommodation. He was in sympathy with the sentiments expressed in the circular, and said it was plain enongh that vessels wore continually kept away from Runcorn owing to want of accommodation. They in Runcorn, should first give their atteetion to bringing trade to the port, and ,then the graving dock would come as a natural coeseqeence. (Applause.)— Mr. Collier said there was very little left for him to say, he thought he should have had the first innings. Speak ing with regard to street making he said he thought the council should employ direct labour. He thought it would he a blexsing to Runcorn if they could do so. They might find work for a number of those at present unemployed. He humorously referred to the gas in Run- corn, and in dealing with sanitary matters he spoke of the nexinus Yapeurs emitted from openferids, and that Dr. RonSP, who had given special attention to the matter. , was of the opinion that it was conducive to diphtheria. He alluded to the better methods in Cardiff and Bristol, and to the low death rate there. Speaking of the Teeknical Institute he said he would have preferred to have seen baths and a recreation ground. They were cramming their youths. It was all mental development, hut they must have physical development to support it. He Was heartily sorry for Runcorn lads. They had not a (tress plot to play on, and no swimming bath in which to learn to swim. He hoped that the Commissioners . would see their way to provide recreation gronnds for the children of Runcorn, to take them off the streets. En sneaking of the craving dook,whilst seeing the necessity of a graving dock, he was greatly in favour of increased lay-by accommodation. He would look after the best interests of Runcorn if again elected. A number of questions were asked, and satisfactorily answered by the candidates. A vote of confidence in Messrs. Imison and Collier was passed unanimously on the proposition of Mr. T. Cook, seconded by Mr. Jephson,and supported by Mr. Mellor. A vote of thanks to the Chairman con- cluded the meeting. The Liberal Council have appealed to the electors te only vote for the candidates who have promised to sup- port the pro.ressivo programme issued by the Council. A list of their candidates has been published. In one ward, four gentlemen are recommended to the gm srs, and five in another ward, but, of course, votes ca!, only be cast for three candidates in each ward. The result of ,he poll will be declared on Monday.

div.head: PELICAN INN. THE MAGISTRATES AND THE PROPOSED ALTERATION.
div.p: THE PELICAN INN. THE MAGISTRATES AND THE PROPOSED ALTERATION.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Monday, Mr. T. Swift, barrister, Liverpool, appeared on behalf of the tenant and licensee (Mr. Fair. Turner), and Messrr. Graenall, Whitley and Co.. the owners of the property to quhmit the clans to the bench for the parthsl rebuild- ing and general improvement of the Pelican Inn, Butter- market-Frt., and Mr. Owen. the architect, was present to give any details the bench might desire. Mr. Swift said the bench would remember that the music license of the " Pelican " was done away with, they would know that upon the right hand side of the premises there was an entry leading into Percival's-fold which con- tained a large number of inhabitants. Up to the present time there had always been a dnoewav from the public- house to the fold, hut his clients had thought that it would be a satisfaction to the beach if the premises were self-contained, and in the plans for the rebuilding of the property that door was entirely done away wilia and there would not be any entry out of the licensed premises into Percival's-fold. Upon the other hand, there was an entry between the public- house and a butcher's shop which was the only building having any communication with the entry, and it was their Dian to make a door at the bottom with a grating in it. In order to remove all objections, and they would put up a door to separate the domestic convenience from that of the customers. There would he no public entrance to the premises ex- cept that at the front in Buttermarkat-et. Their inten- tion was that the people walking out of the house into the 'yard should come hack the same way. The plans included improvements of the premises on the floor level and the increasing of the height of the rooms, but the drinking area was still confined to the four walls. To consider their decision the mag.istrates retired for half-an-hour and on their return the Mayor, who was in the chair, said the Bench would adopt the plans.— Mr. Swift asked that the plans might be signed and one deposited with the Magistrates' Clerk, while they would work imnn the other. Mr. Robert Davies then informed the Bench that he had been instructed by Messrs. Greenall, Whitlss , and Co. to say that with a view of meeting the public con- venience they had made arrangements for the porchase of the warehouse and piece of land on the east side of the " Pelican," and they intended to make a present of this niece of land to the town for the purpose of iin prov- ing the narrow alley known as Percival's-fold.

• HALTON. __— Tim PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.—The minutes of the Halton Parochial Committee came up for consideration at the meeting of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Autho- rity on T esday. The meeting was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom, Halton, on Saturday, the Rev. G. D. Wray in the chair. There were also prEsent Meisrs.T.Wright, Looker, Gamon, Ackerley, J. Farrington (inspector of nuisances). and J. Ashton (clerk). The Clerk sub- mitted and read the report of the medical officer of lie,lth with ieference to Halton Brook which was read* at the previous meeting of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary AuthoritY. It was resolved that a copy thereof be for- warded to the Local Government Board. Ihe Impector reported that Mr. Thomas Golding,of Halton Brook.had connected his drains with the Authority's sewer without- ' permission, and it was resolved that the Clerk should write informing him that he had rendered himself liable to a penalty of £2O, and that unless he disconnected- them, proc.eodings would be instituted. It was decided that £lO. should he paid to the Clerk for his services in connection with the committee, up to the 28th inst. The minutes were adopted on the motion of Mr. Stokes.

LECTURE ON SOUTHER/4 INDIA.—Last evening week a lortir, wag d.liverel in the Infant S;..hoolroom, Pen- b the. Rev. A. A. Dignum of Salem, Madras. Thp lecture, which VPIS illustrated by the aid of a magic lantern, gave an interesting view of the people, their manners and customs, and their religion of Southern Pidia. Special references were made w;th respect to the progress of Christian missions and schools; and, by the aid of the excellent lantern slides supplied by the Lon- don Missionary Society, many beautiful and striking evidences were afforded of the certain advance which is being made in Christian civilization. Mr. W. J. Wig- field, of Home Lea, presided on the occasion, and a col- lection was made at the close of the meeting in aid ol the Salem mission.

div.head: ELECTIONS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THE ELECTIONS AT RUNCORN.

TEIE POLLING ARRANGEMENTS, The Urban District Council election at Runcorn assumed more of a definite aspect on Fridiy, when those who wished to withdraw from the contest did so. Four o'clock was the latest hour appointed for so doing by the returning officer (Mr. Lake), and it was found tlaat'a number of candidates, including several members of the present Board of Commissioners, had handed in withdrawal notices. Only one ward is, however, to go uncontested, and that is Mersey Ward. No fewer than six withdrawal notices were sent in from Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. Abel, Gatley, Handley, Hankinson and Horse- field. This left three candidates for the ward, and as three councillors are required, Messrs. Posnett, Giice, and G. H. Kirkham are thus elected without opposition. —Two canctidates retired from the contest in Haltom ward, viz. : Messrs. Abel and Norman. The remeining candidates to contest this ward are Messrs. S. Taylor, Wiswall, Frith, and Sweetrnen.—ln Central War 1, four candidates withdrew, viz. : Messrs. Gatley, Hankinson, J. H. Kirkham, and A. Norman, thus leaving fee t can- didates in the field. These are DnUastaldi, Meesra. mini- son, Collier, T. Lea, and T. Carr.—Only two candidetes retired from the contest in Bridgewater Ward, these being Messrs. Imison and J. H. Kirkham. The following will contest the ward :—Re Si (Congregational minister), Edward Key, E. Getley, R. Abel, G. Hewitt, and Dr. McKenzie.—Nevrtown ward will be the most het!y contested division, and for the three vacancies there are seven aspirants, viz. : Messrs. D. riisbrown, Jas. Dobson, JAS. Kirkham, T. Reynolds, J. Wilson, Wm. Leach, and W. M. Williams.—Four can- didates withdrew from the contest in Heath ward leav- ing a like plumber to contest the ward. These are Messrs. P. Speakman, J.P., C.C., James Pritchard, J.W. Lightburn and J. Hayes. Mr. Lake has arrange d 'he following polling places for the election nt district councillors, and Poor-law Guar- dians to-morrow (Saturday). The polling booths will open at 12 noon and close at 8 p.m. Helton Ward, 429 electors, Mill Brow Schools; Mersey Ward, 600 electors, Itwo polling booths, New Trades' Union Hall, John-st. ; ' Central Ward, 894 electors, two polling booths, Bruns- wick-st. Schools; Bridgewater Ward, 653 electors, two pollihe booths. Technical Institute, Waterloo-road ; New- town Ward, 648 electors, zwo polling booths, Stiaw-st. Schools; Heath Ward, 424 electors, polling station, Board Schoole, Vi teria-road. THE CANDIDATURE OF MR. BISBROWN. A meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. D. Bisbrown, candidate for Newtown ward, was held in the Primitive Methodist schoolroom on Tuesday evening. There was a good attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr. B. Crosby.—The Chairman said a new era was dawning upon them in reference to the gevernnient of their town, and he hoped there would be increased interest taken in local affairs. He did not think it wae at all creditable to them as ratepayers in the past, that only 20 or 30 per cent of the ratepayers had presented themselves at the polline booths at the election of Com- missioners. That, he thought, was due to the very bad system which was then in vogue. But now with a better system, it was the duty of every man whose name was upon the register to come and record his vote. They had also now the advantage of the town being divided into wards. There were two matters of the utmost importance to them as ratepayers, viz.: every- thing pertaining to the health of the town, and also the trade of the town. He thought any stinting of money in that which pertained to the health of the town was a penny-wise and pound-foolish policy. The question of technical instruction was also a most important one. He was very sorry indeed, and very much surprised, at the way the efforts of the Technical Instruction Com- mittee had been cried down. He thought they owed a debt of gratitude to those who hail werked so hard for the erection of the Technical Institute. (Hear, hear). The speaker then proceeded to give his reasons for sup- portine the candidature of Mr. Bisbrown. which, sum- marised, were—that he was a resident in the ward, that he (the chairman) believed workingmen should he directly represented on the District Council. that Mr. Bisbrown was a workingman, an independent candi- date, a man of experience, and that he had been thoroughly consistent in everything he had done.—Mr. Bisbrown. at the outset of his address, said he wanted to stand on his own merits. He proceeded to give the number of his attendances at the meetings of the Board and the committee meetings since his election in 1891. In the years 1891-2 he attended 89 per cent, of the meetings. in 1892-3. 82 per cent., and 1893.4 he had a' tended 118 board and committee meetings, or 80 per c,enteof the whole. Durine the three years he had attended 291 meetings out of a possible 352. (Applause.) The speaker passed in review the number of matters which had come ueder the consideration of the Board during his term of office, and a number of important matters he had advocated. Referring to the question of baths he said he did not think the time was opportune for the question to come in the forefront, although per- stenally he was in favour of the prevision of the baths. He had always strenuously supported the dividing of the town into wards, and hail advocated the matter in season and out of season. tie thought that now there would be a better supervision of the town. Under the old system that which seemed evervlendy'e business was nobody's business. Speaking of the new Technical Institute he said he was of the opinion that it would be far from being a " white elephant." Its future succene depended upon whom the ratepayers sent to represent them on the District Council. If they appointed a num- ber of workingmen it would be for them to see that it was carried out in a proper manner. If English workers were to hold their own they must go in ler more of that kind of instruction. It was admitted that. several con- tinental countries were far ahead of Ira in this matter of technical instruction, and it behoved them to he stir- ring themeelvesef they were not to lag behind the rest. After dealing comprehensively with the questiee of a graving dock since it was first mentioned in 1881, the communication from the C-nal Company, as published fully in last week's " Examiner," eves read, and also the suggestions of the committee of the Board of Commissioners. He said some people were in favour of the provision of a graving dock, nure and simple, as laid down in the agreement. but whilet he was in favour of such a provision, he did net lose sight of the fat that the exteneion of the lay-by was ahsn- lutely neceseary, and that it would materially help them 111(.7 had another lay-by. The construntion of the Tay-by went& he thought, tend to the prosperity of the town. Some fifty vessels had been di4charreed on the canal between E tstharn and Runcorn since last February and not eV of them had been discharged in Runcorn. Be thought that spoke eloquently of the heed of some extension of their lay-be. The speeker referred to the nece,sity of a read from Runeorn to Weston point, he tleotight would increase trade and be a great adye n There was danger in permit> having to walk clewe the canal think, whirli had been celled a "death trap." swine to the many fatalities which had occurred. Referrire to the rates, he said there had been a. ereat deal of erumhline about them being so high as 2e. 10c1. in the £ He accounted for it by the epidemics they had had, and said they had had to defer several improve- ments to keep the rate at that figure. He also spoke of the action he took for the purchase of the water works. and referred to the satisfactory results of the first :Tar's working. In conclusion he appealed to them for their support on Saturday, and said he wonld endeavour to serve them without fear or favour, as he had endeev- mired to do in the past. (Loud applanee.)—Two ques- tions were atked reletive to the graving dock, and answered by Mr. Biehrown. A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the meeting. MESSRS. IMISON AND COLLIER'S CANDIDATURE. A public meeting in support of the candidature of Mesers. 'Unison and Collier, candidates for the Central ward was held in the Salvation Army Barracks on Wednesday evening. Mr. B. Kniveton neeepiee the chair, and there were also on the platform in addition to the two candidates Messrs. T. Cook, I. Bowyer, R. Wright. J. Davies, T. Caereeill, and Herron. Therew as a very large attendance.—The Chairman said it was very pleasing to see the people taking an interest in the management of the affairs of their own town. The better that interest was,the more likely were they to get good thorough representatiyes.—Mr. imison said they might remember that 15 enonthe since when he stood on the platform in Bethesda schoolroom, seeking election to the Boar:hit was alleged that many properties in Run- corn had been neelected owing to certain influences. It had been suggested that certain gentlemen'e interests were protected.and that it became somebetit'S d IltiES to see that those interests were abolished. That was the particular work his actions had been directed towards whilst on the Board. He was heartily sorry those contests had arisen because it had happened at an awkward time. Everyone Wa,F4 regretting the existence of distress in the town, over which the Commissioners had no control, and it seemed that an spare money would have been better employed in reliev- ing distress than expendine it in elections. But the election took place under different circumstances from an previous one. The old system of voting which had been condemned time after time had been done away with, and they had now the ballot and one man one vote. (Applaose.) A.RRINGTON RAGGED SCHOOL AND MISSION.

The first of a series of limelight entertainments was given in the schoolroom, Bewsey-st., on Satur- day evening, the subject being "Jane's Conquest," followed with other views. Mr. Lewis George kindly contributed the lantern and views, assisted by Mr. Thomas Jones. Mr. H. Osbourne gave the .reading. At the close Mr. Woods gave a solo. Mr. Woodhouse acted as accompanist. There was a good audience.

WORKINGMEN'S MISSION SUNDAY ECHOOL, BANK I QUAY. On Sunday a P.S.A. was held in the above-Earned place. A short address was given by the Superinten- dent, Mr. Joseph Monks, jun., on" habit, &c." Mr. Pawson also made a few remarks. Prizes were given to scholars for early and good attendance, and two duets were well rendered by Miss C. Ashley,and Mr. Samuel Hassall. A solo was rendered by Mr. James Mills with chorus. The service was most enjoy- able.

PRESENTATION TO ORFORD CHURCH.

Mrs. Beamont, of Orford Hall, has presented a beautiful oak altar cross for use in the church. The curate (the Rev. W. R. Hartwright), in acknowledg- ing the gift in the " Parish Magazine " for this month, says :—" We feel very thankful to Mrs. Beamont for this manifest token of sympathy and goodwill. May all as they look upon the Cross realise in all its fullness the glorious redemption of Cli rist." very tasteful calendar has been issued for 1895 by Messrs. E. and A. Eustance, jewellers, Sankey- street. A special lecture on Sick Nursing was given in the Church Institute Moore, on Monday, by Miss Kirby, one of the lecturers appointed by the County Council, and late nurse at the Royal Man- chester Infirmary. The lecturer dealt specially with " surgical nursing," and instructions were given as to the duties of a nurse in eases of acci- dents and operations. Practical demonstrations shewing how to dress simple bruises, cuts, ulcers, &c., were given, and useful information as to how to prepare and apply bandages. There was a good attendances of ladies, and evidently much interest is taken in the lectures. LARGE ASSORTMENT of Furs, newest styles. and choice bkias. —EvANs'. 17, Sankey-street, Warrington.—Advt. PADGATE Y.P.S.C.E.
The inaugural meeting of the newly-formed Wesleyan Young People's Society was held in the Weileyan schoolroom on Monday evening, when the chair was occupied by Mr. W. C. Thornton, of

Frodsham, and there was a large attendance of ladies and gentlemen. Mr. Stewart, the secretary of the Warrington Y.M.C.A., opened the proceed- ings by an address on "Beginning." The Chairman said he was much interested in the movement, be- cause they were forming a similar one at Frodsham, and especially so because of his former connection with Padgate. They could not do too much for their young men. They were the rising generation, and it was to them they had to look to follow in the old people's footsteps. He hoped their society would be a success. Speeches were also delivered by Quartermaster-Sergeant Mantle, Mr. H. Harring- ton, and Mr. H. E. Roscoller. Songs were credit- ably rendered during the evening by Miss Bennett and Mr. Hassall, and violin solos by Miss K. Cooper. BOLD-ST. WESLEYAN SERvICES FOR THE PEOPLE. At the" People's Service" which was held in the Bold-street Wesleyan Church on Sunday afternoon, I the Rev. G. D. Mason occupied the chair. Theta I was a large congregation which gave frequent mani- festations ot its appreciation of the programme and of the manner in which it was gone through. The address was given by the Rev. J. Kirtlan, who spoke of the "Providence of God." "Light in Thirkness " was sung with good effect by Miss Collin and tilt; orchestral band played in their usual excellent style, a minuet from Samson," Cujus anima ns "from Stabat Mater, and "Gloria." I L.,

The present season in connection with these con- certs was opened on Saturday evening at the Co- operative Hall, Sankey-st. This is the fifth season, and they commenced under very favourable aus- pices, there being a large audience, and the chair was occupied by Mr. John Fairclough, J.P. Ihe chairman said he was glad to be present on that, the first concert of the season, and was pleased to see such a large attendance. He hoped, and had no doubt, that the concerts would be as successful in every way as they bad proved in former years. A good programme having been provided was ren- dered in a manner which left nothing to be desirei. A Grand larch, by Mr. Kirk's reed band, proved an excellent ctart to the evening's performance, for which they were heartily applauded. "Dream Faces ".and a "Spanish dance," were rendered by the same party with a like result. Miss Cosgrove was very happy in her songs, "By the Fountain." and "Jack O'Hazledene," for which she was awarded very warm applause. Mr. John Parkinson sang with good taste and effect, " Rivals " and "The Forge." Mr. W. H. Wallington sang "The Scout," I and "Four jolly Smiths," being encored be gave "The red Jacket." The humorist of the evening was Mr. A. Grounds, who is a great favourite with a Warrington audience. He introduced for the first time his two life sizelgures, and by his genius humour and wit, kept the audience in continuous hilarity. giss S. Hamilton Bradbury, and Miss Grounds were the accompanists. Mr. S. B. Stringer thanked the chairman and all who had taken part, and thus a very bright evening was brought to close.

div.head: ASSAULT AT AIMS AT NEWTON.
div.p: ASSAULT AT AIMS AT NEWTON.

On Thursday evening before a very large audience the members of the Earlestown, Newton and District Gymnasium, assisted by three members of the Liver- pool Gymnasium, gave a special display of gymnastics in the Town Hall, Newton. Mr. Robert Stone presided, and he was accompanied on the platform by Messrs. R. Stuart, R. Barton, C. H. Bedmer, Captain Royse, and Dr. Watkins, and a number of ladies. The Chairman said they were assembled there to witness an assault at arms by the Newton Gymnastic Club. The classes were first started at Earlestown 12 months ago by Mr. Brun- ton, and a few gentlemen associated with him. He was informed that in their first season they had between 50 land 60 members, about 35 being from Earlestown and 25 from Newton. Mr. Brunton, Mr. Cook, the hon. secretary, and the member: of the committee having as- certained that they conld take the Newton Town Hall, and that it was suitable for their requirements, they determined to commence their second season there, and the performance which they would witness that night would terminate that season. The ladies' class had been a decided success, having upwards of 45 mem- bers, and they had been compelled to start two classes. Ile thought that spoke well, and should, he considered, be an incentive to everybody to take an interest in the gymnasium, when they saw ladies coming forward in this way. The Earlestown members had fallen away, but the Newton members were just the same as those who walked to Earlestown last year. Englishmen had al- ways delighted in being in the front of athletic games of all kinds,and among the counties of England,hethought Lancashire had taken a prominent position. (Applause). He hoped these classes started in a very mociorate way, would be the means of seeing a proper gymnasium storted, arid that whenever that time came they should find men amongst them who would maintain the position ' which Lancashire had gained.—(Applause).—The pro- gramme which was gone through included horizontal ' and parallel bars, rings, high jnmping, rope climbing, wrestling, boxing competitions for strength, and tugs of war. Each of the items was well executed, and the audience were not sparing in their applause. The com- petition for a silver medal given by Mr. R. Brunton, for the competitor who could show his chin the greatest number of times above the horizontal bars, was won by J. Hodnett (35).

div.head: EA RLESTOW.N GOOD TEMPLARS.
div.p: EA RLESTOW.N GOOD TEMPLARS.

-- The members of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars paid a visit to the " Coneilio et labore Lodge, Manchester, on Saturday last. The party, num- bering ever 50, arrived at their destination at 3 p.m., and after spending a few hours viewing the sights of the " City " assembled in the Wesleyan School, Lever-st., where tea was provided. After tea the lodge was opened, and the visitors were heartily welcomed, Bro. George E. Warburton, C.T., being invited to preside, supported by the officers of the Earlestown Lodge. Earnest addresses were given by the Chairman, and Bro. W. H. Dale, C.C.T., and an excellent programme of piano solos, songs, recitations, &c.. was very satisfac- torily rendered by Bros. W. Willis, George Roberts, Jas. Huddleston, George Clarke, Win. Wilson, George E. Warburton and sisters, Mrs. Willis, Miss Roberts, Miss R. Cordingley, R. Warburton, E. Travis. Thanks were accorded the visitors, and a very enjoyable meeting closed at 930. The usual weekly sessinn of the Lodge was held in the Co-operative Hall on Monday night when there was a very large attendance of members and visitors,the latter including Bro. Q.M. Sergeant Roberts, of Warrington. Bro. George E. Warburton, C.T., presided. Three can- didates were initiated and six proposed for membership. Several items of business affecting the internal working of the Lodge were transacted after which th-. programme of the evening was introduced,married members being re- sponsible. Ham sandwiches and other refreshments were handed round to all present, and a very pleasant and enjoyable evening was spent in a social manner. Thanks were accorded those providing the entertainment on the motion of Bro. Joseph Anderton, seconded by Bro. J. H. Willia mu.

RUNCORN URBkN DISTRICT COUNCIL. ELECTION. 1894. TO THE ELECTORS OF HEATH WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,— I offer myself as a Candidate for the above Ward at the issuing Election. The additional powt re granted to the Urba.nDistriet Coun- cil should. in my opinion, be exercised with the view of thoughtful development and not to sensational effect. Two of the essentials of human happiness are Health and Employment. With a view of giving an index to my future action, lam reluctantly compelled to refer to the past. In connection with Sanitary Matters, I moved for the formation ot a Health Committee for Run ern, and was for many years its first Chairman ; I was also Chairman of the first Baths' Committee which made an exhaustive enquiry and aid all that was then possible to procure th 3 great blessing of Baths for the town. Three years since, when I was re-elected a member of the now expiring Board of Commissioners, I suggested Deep Do2ks as an absolute necessity for Runcorn; I with others could not obtain this desideratum, but we secured the lesser benefit of a Lay-by. With the gloomy outlook in the Chemical Trade, the energies of the newly-elected District Council should be especially directed to the development of the Shipping Inter- est and its dependent Trades. The competition of Elleamare Port and other places makes this subject of the most vital Importance to Runcorn. Absolute pledges cannot be given, but in the present negotiations with the Manchester Ship Canal Company, I will, in case I am favoured with your confidence, endeavour to give effect to these views. As very many of the Voters in Heath Ward have qualifica- tions in other Districts, it is most advisable that electors should Vote for the Ward in which they reside. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen Yours vey y respectfully, JOHN W. LIGHTBURN. Heath House, Runcorn, Dec Bth. 1894.

RUNCORN URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL ELECTION. TO THE ELECTORS OF HEATH WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,— The passing of the Local Govornment Bill brings us face to face with a new era in municipal government, and the Board of Commissioners now gives place to a Distriet Council. 1 Another matter new to Runcorn is the division of the town into wards. This is a subject that has engaged my earnest attention. I was honoured by the Cheshire County ' touncil to be one of the commi: tee ti conduct the inquiry ' with refer•nce to the suSject. and their recommendation was appioved by the Council. This, in my opinion, will enable I the electors to have more complete control over their repre- sentatives, as they mill be able to straw their a' tention to any matters requiring the consideration tat' the District Council. My views on the subject of education gene ally are well known to you. I consider it absolutely necessary that the young people of the present day shou!cl have the fell benefits arising from the grants which the County Council are now giving, and it is eminently satisfactory to find that -Runcorn ia in the front rank of all urban districts, as they have been recipients of net simply yearly grants for the purposes of higher education, but a handsome turn towards the new Technical Institute, which is apt,roaehing completion My sincere hope is that full es:vantage will be taken of the opportunities provided by the new Institute by I these wishing to make progress in the worts]. My dual position as a Commissioner and County Councillor has enabled me to leok after the true interests of the town in this matter and you may rely upon the best interests of Run- I corn receiving in the future, as in the past,my best care and attention. You are all aware of the great depression that exists- at the present moment In the town, and one of the things that I think will facilitate an improvement is the immediate carry- ing out of the egreement of September, 1890. existing between the Commissioners and the Ship Canal Co_ with respect to the provision of a graving do..k. I have hitherto cealortsly ' laboured to bring this about, and sh 1 confiner' my -efforts to , this end, so that vessels arrivine at Runoorn will not ,be com- pelled to go elsewhsre for repairs. This will revive an old industry that gave labour to a large number of carpenters and others. The acquisition of the Water Works by the Commissioners has proved of desisted benefit to the town, for, although numerous difficult ics have been encountered during the first year. a substantial profit has resulted. This bears out my expressed anticipations when the scheme was considered by you. The health of the town is on. deserving the closest atten- tion of your representatives. and the increase I activity co the part of the Health Committee during thepast two years has met with my warmest suppset The resfuct on in the death-rate of late must be gratifying h- all of you. All sani- tary improvements shall always rec Ave my earnest atten- tion. There are many other subjects which will call for the attention of your representatives,which will include, amongst others, the provision of a recreation ground. This has my entire sympathy;and shall receive, together with all matters affe ding the best interests of the town, my most earnest consideration. It must have been gratifying to you, as ratepayers, to have found your burdens somewhat lightened by the c.:ntribution of a further £2OO a year. making ire all, £4OO per annum by the County Council for the maintenance of the main roads of the town. I confidently appeal to you for a renewal of your confi- dence which has been uninterrupted for over twenty years, and if elected upon the new Urban District Council. you may rely upon my best efforts being devoted to carefully 'watch all matters concerning the welfare and advancement of our town. lam, Lades and Gentlemen, Yours laithfully, PHILIP SPEAKMAN. The Mount, Higher Runcorn, 29th, November, 1894.

LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, Havinff beea urged by a number of Electors in the Ward to allow myself to be nominated, I have, after careful consideration, consented so to do. As to my qualifications for the office. I be,,y, in the first instance to remind you that I have be-ea for many years a tradesman and ratepayer in the to VI.I, and consequently am fully convetsant with the needs thereof. Secondly, having practically retired from business, I have leisure at my dis- posal which I am ready and willing to devote to the further. ance of our mutual interests. And as to S tnitary questions, I think I may without egotism claim to have a thorough practical knowle Age of such matters. In the matter of general Improvements, I should prefer to " make haste slowly," as in my opinion, owing to the great deptebsion in trade, it woull not b 3 wise to materially increase the rates. As regirds the accommodation for Shipping which the Manchester S'tip Canal Company undertook to provide, I think the present time most opportune for proceeding with the work, as there is every likelihood otherwise of the num- ber of unemployed being greatly augmented. All other questions affecting the welfare of the town will have my careul attention, and I trust, in the event of being elected to the Council. the votes I may record will not fail to give you satisfaction. • I am, Ladi,s and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, JAMES KIRKHAM. TO THE ELECTORS OF STOCKTON HEATH. ELECTION OF DISTRICT COUNCILLOR. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, I have issued to you my a idress as Candidate for the Parish Council. but in addition to this I ALSO seek your suffrages as DISTRICT COUNCILLOR. I may briefly say that the powers of the District Council are the greater, and it is because that in this capacity I can exert myself to greater usefulness that I offer myself. For some years past the Ashpits of Stockton Heath have been a great nuisance and inconvenience to the inhabitants. Twelve months ago I waited upo, Os, Parochial Committee to ask them to take steps to remedy this evil, but I received no satisfaction from them. I then visited the Rural Sanitary Authority at Duttan with the came result, I then, at my own expense, instructed a solicitor to bring the matter before the Lo •el Government Bard, I also sent a petition to this body, and after six months' correspondence, the result is the authorities now empty the Ashpits. My efforts to improve the Sanitary conditions of the district are well-known, and the correspondence as to the above matters I should be pleased to show to any interested person. The District Council having the control of the highways, if you do me the honour to return me, one of my acts will be to endeavour to prevent the an,:oy ence and inconvenience that is now caused to the Inhabitants of Stockton Heath by the Swing Bridge being kept open an unnecessarily long time, as is now the case. The Act gives the power, and I should strenuously oppose the enclosure of common lands and roadside wastes.
